13.5 Model-Specific Attack Vectors

A stop sign with strategically placed black and white stickers can remain recognizable to a human while an evaluated image classifier labels it as a speed limit sign. The attacker changes the observed input rather than the classifier’s code or stored weights. This adversarial example illustrates why the lifecycle entry point matters. Training data, model artifacts, and runtime inputs give an attacker different ways to influence the system and require controls at different boundaries.

The lifecycle entry point separates five objectives. Model theft targets confidentiality by obtaining artifacts or reproducing behavior from queries. Output leakage targets the training data, which the same queries can expose through the predictions the service is authorized to return. Poisoning targets training integrity by changing what the model learns. Adversarial examples target deployed behavior by changing the inputs a model receives. Availability abuse uses the same serving interface to exhaust the service’s compute and cost budget rather than to change any prediction. Data poisoning therefore requires an intervention in the learning pipeline, whereas adversarial inputs and availability abuse call for controls on the deployed service. Written as the four-field threat model of section 13.4, the objectives differ mainly in asset and adversary capability. Theft targets weights or behavior and needs either artifact access or query access, and output leakage targets the training data with nothing more than query access. Poisoning targets training integrity and needs write access to something the model learns from. Adversarial inputs target deployed decisions and need control over an input, while availability abuse targets the serving budget and needs nothing beyond an account. These objectives connect the attack surface analysis in section 13.4.1 to the controls available before training, during artifact handling, and at inference, while section 13.5.5 examines how token-stream architectures fuse instructions, untrusted content, and retrieved data across those objectives.

These entry points sit at different stages of the ML lifecycle (figure 4). Upstream, an attacker may inject samples or alter labels in a data source the pipeline accepts. A backdoor can then remain inactive on ordinary evaluation inputs and activate on a chosen trigger. Downstream, deployed files expose an artifact-access boundary, while prediction APIs expose a query boundary. An adversarial input crosses the latter without requiring the attacker to alter the training pipeline.

Controls must act at the relevant entry point and preserve their assumptions through later stages. Data validation limits what enters training, artifact controls authenticate what deployment loads, and serving controls constrain requests and returned information. None establishes behavioral correctness by itself; the threat model determines which attack each control must withstand.

13.5.1 Model theft

A competitor spending a few thousand dollars on public API queries to train a surrogate model, or an insider copying unencrypted weights from a bucket, can replicate a model that cost millions of dollars to train (Oliynyk et al. 2023). Model theft, the first of those five objectives, targets confidentiality by recovering a trained model’s parameters, architecture, or output behavior, undermining its economic value or exposing private information encoded in its weights.

Ateniese, G., L. V. Mancini, A. Spognardi, A. Villani, D. Vitali, and G. Felici. 2015. “Hacking Smart Machines with Smarter Ones: How to Extract Meaningful Data from Machine Learning Classifiers.” International Journal of Security and Networks 10 (3): 137. https://doi.org/10.1504/ijsn.2015.071829.

3 Model serialization: Python’s pickle format, common in PyTorch checkpoint workflows, can execute arbitrary code during deserialization, so loading an untrusted checkpoint is equivalent to running untrusted code. Formats such as SafeTensors store only tensor data and remove that execution path (Hugging Face 2026).

Hugging Face. 2026. Safetensors Documentation.

Such threats arise across a range of deployment settings, including public APIs, cloud-hosted services, on-device inference engines, and shared model repositories. Prediction interfaces can leak enough signal to recover model functionality (Tramèr et al. 2016; Oliynyk et al. 2023), while classifier outputs can reveal meaningful information about training sets or learned structure (Ateniese et al. 2015). Artifact handling introduces separate risks. Unsafe deserialization3 can execute attacker-supplied code, while insufficient access controls can expose model files or deployment packages directly.

Model theft pursues two distinct objectives, and each requires different controls (figure 5). Exact artifact theft obtains the model file or deployment artifact through storage, registry, or device access. The attacker can reuse the recovered weights without repeating their training. Approximate behavioral theft uses API responses, such as labels, logits, embeddings, or confidence scores, to train a surrogate. It can exploit permitted queries without breaking authentication. The literature names this query-based branch in several ways. Model extraction and model stealing are synonyms for the attack, while knockoff modeling and model distillation name its usual training step, in which a surrogate learns from the victim’s outputs. Its usual product is a behavioral surrogate, but the same query access can also recover selected internal parameters, a third outcome that the OpenAI results below demonstrate. Encryption, access control, and protected deployment paths restrict artifact access; signatures separately authenticate artifact integrity. Output limits, query budgets, auditing, and pricing constrain behavioral extraction, while watermarking can support attribution after copying.

Definition 13.3: Model extraction

Model extraction is the class of attacks in which an adversary, with only black-box query access to a deployed model’s prediction interface, recovers the model’s parameters, decision boundaries, or behavior by analyzing observable outputs.

  1. Significance: Successful extraction often costs orders of magnitude less than the original training. Published demonstrations have recovered logistic regression, neural-network, and decision-tree models from public machine-learning APIs with high fidelity and modest query cost (Tramèr et al. 2016). Later work has reconstructed components of large language models, including OpenAI deployments studied by Carlini et al. (2024), using only public query access. The BERT extraction example below illustrates the same dynamic on a transformer model, using only synthetic queries to train the copy.
  2. Distinction: Extraction differs from direct theft of model files (which requires intrusion into the storage layer) and from model inversion (which uses model outputs to infer training-data properties or reconstruct representative inputs rather than the model itself). Its attack surface is the model’s query interface, so every deployed ML service faces it by construction whenever the model is reachable.
  3. Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that rate limiting alone is a sufficient defense. An attacker willing to issue queries slowly, distribute requests across accounts, or accept a multi-month attack window may still extract useful behavior. Reducing output information, detecting systematic probing, and pricing queries can raise the cost or expose the attempt, but their combination does not guarantee prevention.

Model theft can also enable attacks on information encoded by the model. Extraction studies demonstrate recovery of useful behavior or selected internal parameters, although those outcomes do not imply complete replication of a large model or its training pipeline (Tramèr et al. 2016; Carlini et al. 2024). A competitor holding a stolen Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) recommendation model obtains its embedding tables, which store a learned vector for each value of each categorical feature. In a recommender those features commonly include user and item IDs, so the stolen tables hand the competitor a per-user vector shaped by that user’s history, a natural starting point for inferring the user’s attributes. Whether this exposes particular customer attributes depends on the model, accessible features, and auxiliary information. Model inversion attacks investigate that boundary by attempting to infer sensitive input properties from the learned model (section 13.5.2.2). Even when the artifact itself remains secured, the approximate behavioral extraction path in figure 5 becomes practical because black-box query cost can be much lower than the cost of training the original model.

Example 13.1: The BERT model extraction
Scenario: Proprietary language models deployed behind public inference APIs return full probability vectors and confidence scores to client queries (Krishna et al. 2020).

Diagnosis: The attacker needed no real training data. Because both the victim and the copy were fine-tuned from the same publicly released pretrained BERT, queries made of random word sequences shaped by simple task-specific heuristics supplied enough labeled outputs to train a student. That student recovered much of the victim’s task performance on tasks including natural language inference and question answering (Krishna et al. 2020). With a shared public starting point, the API responses had to supply only the task-specific fine-tuning signal. Retaining task accuracy is distinct from agreeing with the target on each input; neither implies recovery of its exact parameters.

Systems lesson: API endpoints expose intellectual property when outputs carry raw decision-boundary logits. Serving platforms combine rate-limiting, query auditing, and confidence-score truncation to make model extraction more costly and detectable.

Krishna, Kalpesh, Gaurav Singh Tomar, Ankur P. Parikh, Nicolas Papernot, and Mohit Iyyer. 2020. “Thieves on Sesame Street! Model Extraction of BERT-Based APIs.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Exact artifact theft

Exact artifact theft targets the model’s stored structure and learned parameters. The exposed path may be an artifact-download API, an on-device inference package, or a model repository. This differs from querying a prediction API: the attacker obtains the artifact itself. Weak access control or unprotected packaging can expose that artifact without requiring full control of the underlying infrastructure.

The value of a stolen artifact depends on what it contains and what the attacker wants to reproduce. Learned parameters and architecture details can support inference when the necessary preprocessing and runtime are available. Training hyperparameters, including learning rate schedules, batch sizes, and regularization settings, help reproduce or extend training, but are not required merely to execute an existing checkpoint. Side-channel attacks,4 reverse engineering, or analysis of observable outputs may reveal additional structure when the artifact is incomplete. The threat model should therefore distinguish running a copied model from rebuilding the pipeline that produced it.

4 ML side-channel attacks: Timing or power observations can reveal properties of inference even when model files and query outputs are restricted. Recovering useful structure depends on the implementation, measurement access, and signal quality; physical proximity is a precondition for some channels, not a guarantee of success.

Tramèr, Florian, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels, Michael K Reiter, and Thomas Ristenpart. 2016. “Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs.” 25th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 16), 601–18.
Oliynyk, Daryna, Rudolf Mayer, and Andreas Rauber. 2023. “I Know What You Trained Last Summer: A Survey on Stealing Machine Learning Models and Defences.” ACM Computing Surveys 55 (14s): 1–41. https://doi.org/10.1145/3595292.

System designers must account for these risks by separating artifact security from interface security. Artifact controls secure model files, registry entries, and deployment packages; interface controls restrict APIs, reduce output precision, audit query patterns, and price or rate-limit access so behavioral extraction becomes harder to perform economically (Tramèr et al. 2016; Oliynyk et al. 2023).

Insider theft of engineering assets

Insider access is often the shortest path to artifact theft, because an insider needs no exploit to reach files that the development environment already grants. The two cases below involve documents and source code rather than model weights, and that difference is their lesson. The protected asset extends beyond the serialized model to the code and data that produced it. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski was accused of taking proprietary Waymo materials before founding a competing startup (The New York Times 2017), a case about engineering intellectual property rather than demonstrated extraction of model weights. In March 2019, Tesla filed two trade-secret lawsuits involving former employees who left for autonomous-vehicle competitors (Korosec 2019). One complaint alleged that employees who joined Zoox copied proprietary warehousing, logistics, and inventory-control documents. A separate complaint alleged that former Autopilot engineer Guangzhi Cao copied Tesla Autopilot source-code repositories before joining XPeng/XMotors.

The New York Times. 2017. Google’s Self-Driving Car Company Sues Uber over Trade Secrets. The New York Times.
Korosec, Kirsten. 2019. Tesla Sues Former Employees, Zoox for Alleged Trade Secret Theft. TechCrunch.

These allegations matter for ML systems because training code, feature pipelines, labeling workflows, deployment scripts, simulation assets, and operational playbooks can reveal enough about a system to accelerate a competitor’s replication effort or expose downstream security weaknesses. API-level extraction defenses do not reach this boundary. Restricting prediction queries cannot prevent a developer from copying repositories that the developer can already access. Development access, artifact handling, and release provenance therefore belong in the same threat model as inference interfaces, with controls matched to the sensitivity of each asset.

Query-based extraction

Approximate behavioral theft uses observed input-output pairs to train a substitute without copying the target’s parameters. This application of model distillation, or knockoff modeling, can reproduce useful functionality from public API responses (Orekondy et al. 2019).

Orekondy, Tribhuvanesh, Bernt Schiele, and Mario Fritz. 2019. “Knockoff Nets: Stealing Functionality of Black-Box Models.” 2019 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 4949–58. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2019.00509.

Evaluation must distinguish task performance from agreement with the victim. A substitute can achieve similar benchmark accuracy while making different predictions; reproducing the victim’s correct answers and mistakes measures behavioral fidelity. The service therefore has to limit accumulated observations while preserving the outputs legitimate users need.

Query access can also expose internal parameters rather than only supply examples for a surrogate. In their paper, Carlini et al. (2024) show how to reconstruct the final embedding projection matrix of OpenAI’s ada and babbage models, and to recover the hidden dimensionality (and estimate the cost of full matrix recovery) for gpt-3.5-turbo, using only public API access. That final projection maps a hidden state vector to a much larger token vocabulary, so every output logit vector lies in a linear subspace whose rank equals the model’s hidden dimension. Collecting logit vectors across enough varied prompts until new responses become linearly dependent on earlier ones reveals where the rank saturates and recovers the hidden dimensionality. For the smaller models, solving for a basis of that subspace replicates the weight matrix up to affine transformations. This partial parameter extraction is distinct from both copying a complete artifact and training a behavioral substitute. It stops short of recovering the full model, yet it shows that an API’s exposed scores and query controls can reveal internal structure that its operator intended to keep private.

Carlini, N., D. Paleka, K. D. Dvijotham, T. Steinke, J. Hayase, A. F. Cooper, K. Lee, et al. 2024. “Stealing Part of a Production Language Model.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2403.06634.

The empirical results in table 4 demonstrate extraction of smaller models’ output-projection parameters with root mean square errors on the order of \(10^{-4}\), while the larger GPT-3.5 rows show dimension recovery and estimated recovery costs rather than implemented weight-matrix extraction. The production-interface attack used features such as top-\(\TopClassCount\) token log-probabilities together with logit-bias controls. Because a production API returns only the top-\(\TopClassCount\) log-probabilities rather than the full vocabulary vector, the caller can apply a positive logit bias to selected tokens to force them into the top-\(\TopClassCount\) set and read their relative logit values across prompts. The interaction between returned information and permitted query modifications therefore belongs in the threat model, even when neither feature exposes weights directly.

Defenses against model extraction

Unlike data poisoning and adversarial perturbations, whose algorithmic defenses are developed in Robust AI, and training-data leakage, whose formal privacy bounds are developed in section 13.9, model extraction is countered directly at the serving API boundary. This subsection therefore develops the chapter’s complete quantitative treatment of API-level extraction defenses alongside the attack, leaving section 13.8.2 to cover artifact custody, cryptographic packaging, and endpoint authentication infrastructure. Model extraction defenses must account for what an adversary can accumulate through the API across four operational levers. Reducing output precision or returning fewer classes restricts the observations supplied by each response. Query quotas constrain collection per credential, and pricing increases its cost. Behavioral monitoring supplies evidence of systematic probing that can trigger investigation or enforcement. A daily rate limit only slows collection without bounding its lifetime total, and an attacker can combine observations from several accounts. The defense must therefore connect output design to cumulative budgets and the identities over which those budgets can actually be enforced.

Monitoring supplies evidence for adjusting those controls. High query volume is one possible signal, although legitimate batch jobs can produce it and an extractor can deliberately slow collection. A high-traffic, general-purpose prediction API might begin with an illustrative volume rule:

\[ \text{alert}(\text{user}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \DailyAccountQueryCount> 10{,}000 \text{ or } \HourlyAccountQueryCount> 2{,}000 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

where \(\DailyAccountQueryCount\) and \(\HourlyAccountQueryCount\) represent query counts. Such thresholds are only the first signal. They must be calibrated by service tier and by the shape of normal use, because batch customers and attackers can both generate high volume.

The next signal compares the inputs with expected use. Synthetic or systematically varied queries may reveal probing, but an extractor can also submit ordinary examples. A detector can compare the user’s query distribution with a baseline chosen for the service and customer workload:

\[ \KlDivergence(\AccountQueryDistribution\lVert \ExpectedQueryDistribution) > \ResponseThreshold \]

where \(\KlDivergence\) is Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and \(\ResponseThreshold\) is an alert threshold. A practical detector needs a tractable representation of inputs and enough observations to estimate those distributions. For a language model API, unusual token distributions or repetitive prompt templates may provide useful features. Regular inter-query intervals can add evidence of automation, but legitimate applications also automate requests and attackers can vary their timing.

An anomaly detector combines these signals into a score that can drive enforcement:

\[ \text{score}_{\text{anomaly}}(\ApiAccount) = \ExtractionAnomalyClassifier(\text{qps}(\ApiAccount), \KlDivergence(\ApiAccount), \InterQueryIntervalDeviation(\ApiAccount), \ldots) \]

where \(\ExtractionAnomalyClassifier\) is a trained classifier and the features capture query volume, distribution, and temporal regularity. The score supports a response policy rather than establishing that theft occurred. A service can tighten quotas, request additional verification, or refer activity for review, with thresholds calibrated against legitimate workload variation. Free, paid, and enterprise tiers can carry different limits, but account-level enforcement constrains an adversary only to the extent that collection across credentials is also controlled.

A concrete quota ladder for the same general-purpose API makes that information cap visible. A free tier might allow 1,000 queries/day with a 10 queries/s burst, a basic paid tier might allow 100,000 queries/day with 100 queries/s, and an enterprise tier might allow 10M queries/day with custom burst limits and contractual monitoring. The exact numbers depend on product needs, but the ladder matters because extraction cost scales with accumulated responses.

An illustrative adaptive policy connects the anomaly score to a request limit. Higher scores reduce the quota, so false positives translate directly into lost capacity for legitimate workloads:

\[ \text{limit}_{\text{effective}}(\ApiAccount) = \text{limit}_{\text{base}} \times \exp(-\QuotaReductionSensitivity\cdot \text{score}_{\text{anomaly}}(\ApiAccount)) \]

where \(\QuotaReductionSensitivity\) controls sensitivity. With \(\QuotaReductionSensitivity=1\), a user with anomaly score 0.8 keeps about 45 percent of the base quota, a 55 percent rate reduction. The calculation specifies enforcement strength, not detection accuracy. Its security effect also depends on the response: full logits, hidden states, or detailed confidence scores can make each permitted query more useful to an extractor. Quota design therefore needs an explicit output contract.

Output shaping reduces the leakage per response while preserving the part of the answer legitimate users usually need. Confidence rounding returns coarser probabilities instead of full-precision logits or probabilities:

\[ \RoundedClassProbability_i = \text{round}(\PredictedClassProbability_i, \RoundingDecimalCount) \]

where \(\RoundingDecimalCount\) is the number of decimal places. For a 1000-class ImageNet classifier, rounding from 6 decimals to 2 decimals removes 4 decimal digits, about 13.3 bits per class. The count uses a decimal-bin model, which treats each decimal digit as selecting one of ten equally likely levels, so every dropped digit removes \(\log_2 10 \approx 3.3\) bits. This counts representational precision, not measured information about the model. Rounding can also create score ties, so the service must evaluate the effect on ranking and downstream decisions.

The top-\(\TopClassCount\) truncation defense returns only the top-\(\TopClassCount\) predicted classes rather than the full probability distribution:

\[ \text{output} = \{(\ReturnedClassLabel_i, \PredictedClassProbability_i) : \LabelCategoryIndex\in \text{top-}\TopClassCount\} \]

For \(\TopClassCount=\) 5 on a 1000-class problem, the API returns only those top scores instead of the full softmax vector, eliminating 99.5 percent of the distribution entries an extractor could otherwise observe per query. Legitimate users often need only the top few predictions, while an extractor benefits from the full distribution.

Top-\(\TopClassCount\) truncation exposes far fewer scores per query than the full distribution.

When rounded or truncated outputs still leak too much, calibrated noise can make repeated measurements less useful. Adding Gaussian noise to the score vector \(\PredictedOutput\) of a \(\Glyph{K}\)-class model (uppercase \(\ClassCount\) for the class count, distinct from the \(\Glyph{k}\) of top-\(\TopClassCount\)) can push some scores below zero, so the noisy vector is projected back onto a valid probability distribution:

\[ \NoisyClassProbabilityVector=\SimplexProjection\!\left(\PredictedOutput+\ScoreNoiseVector\right), \qquad \ScoreNoiseVector\sim\GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector,\ScoreNoiseStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix) \]

where \(\SimplexProjection\) returns the closest valid distribution to the noisy vector, one whose scores are all nonnegative and sum to one \((\NoisyClassProbability_i\geq 0,\ \sum_i\NoisyClassProbability_i=1)\). The set of such vectors is the probability simplex \(\ProbabilitySimplex^{\ClassCount-1}\). The noise scale \(\ScoreNoiseStandardDeviation\) must balance extraction defense with utility preservation. Too little noise leaves the confidence surface measurable; too much noise changes decisions for legitimate users. This randomized response shaping is not, by itself, a differential privacy guarantee: such a claim also requires an adjacency relation, a sensitivity bound, calibrated noise, and composition accounting.

Differential privacy addresses a different objective when a response is computed from sensitive records. It bounds the change in the released distribution under a specified change to the protected data. Section 13.9 develops the full \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) definition and the adjacent-dataset notation. Repeated interactive DP releases compose, but queries to a fixed DP-trained model are post-processing and do not consume additional training privacy budget. Such queries may still enable model extraction, so output shaping and rate limits remain security controls even when no additional DP loss is incurred.

The final lever is economics. Consider a simplified comparison in which extraction and independent training produce equally useful substitutes and query charges represent the extraction cost. If training from scratch costs \(\TrainingCost\) and extraction requires \(\ExtractionQueryCount\) queries at price \(\QueryPrice\) per query, extraction is the cheaper option when:

\[ \ExtractionQueryCount\cdot \QueryPrice< \TrainingCost \]

Setting \(\QueryPrice\) so that \(\ExtractionQueryCount\cdot \QueryPrice> \TrainingCost\) makes extraction costlier than independent training in this simplified equal-quality comparison. It does not remove incentives based on unavailable training data, competitive value, or objectives other than acquiring a substitute cheaply. For example, if training a competitive large model costs $5M and extraction requires 100M queries, the break-even price is $0.05/query; pricing above that makes extraction more expensive than retraining under those assumptions. The comparison must include the attacker’s alternative costs of compute, data, and engineering. In practice, pricing, monitoring, quotas, and output shaping work together. Restricted outputs and coarse confidence bins reduce exposed detail, while quotas constrain access through the identities they cover. Neither control alone bounds all information an actor can accumulate across accounts, alternate endpoints, or other sources.

Napkin Math 13.1: Protecting a production API
Problem: For a production ResNet-50 image-classification API serving 1M daily queries from 10,000 users, how can the operator make model extraction economically unattractive without degrading normal service?

Scenario: The model costs about $5K to train in this scenario. An extractor needs about 5M queries for 90 percent fidelity, or 5,000 queries/class for a 1,000-class classifier. Without defenses, an attacker abusing a free tier can send 25K queries/day for 200 days and pay nothing, making extraction economically favorable. The service is far smaller than the general-purpose API above, so its tiers and alert thresholds are scaled to its own traffic, and its training cost sits three orders of magnitude below the large model of the break-even example.

Mechanism: The defense stack works as a sequence:

  1. Cap collection: The free tier allows 100 queries/day, the paid tier costs $50/month for 10K queries/day, and enterprise access requires authentication plus monitoring.
  2. Monitor probing: The monitoring path watches for systematic measurement behavior, including more than 5K queries/day from one user or median inter-query gaps below 100 ms; the lightweight detector adds 2 ms per query.
  3. Shape outputs: Output shaping rounds confidences to 2 decimal places, retaining about 6.7 bits from each rounded scalar probability, and returns only the top-5 classes, eliminating 99.5 percent of distribution entries.
  4. Price extraction: At pay-as-you-go $0.001/query (above tier caps), 5M extraction queries cost $5K, matching the training cost in this scenario. An attacker limited to the $50/month tier (10K queries/day) would need 500 days and about $833 total, which is cheaper under these assumptions. A daily quota slows collection but does not cap its lifetime total.
  5. Cap cumulative collection: A per-principal lifetime budget closes that route. If each principal’s queries beyond an allowance well below 5M are billed at the pay-as-you-go $0.001/query, assembling the full extraction set costs close to $5K on any tier, the same as training the model.

Outcomes to measure: Whether the design works is decided by four measurements, namely the surrogate’s accuracy, the accuracy legitimate users still receive, the latency the controls add, and the share of users flagged by mistake. The values below are constructed inputs that show the shape of that measurement, not results derived from the controls above. Suppose the surrogate’s accuracy drops from 90 percent without defenses to 72 percent with defenses, an 18 percentage-point reduction, while legitimate top-5 accuracy remains 99.2 percent, close to the 99.3 percent baseline. Monitoring and output shaping add 2.5 ms on top of 100 ms inference, or 2.5 percent overhead, while flagging 0.3 percent of users for manual review.

Systems insight: Tier caps, monitoring, and output shaping slow an extractor; only the cumulative budget makes the full extraction set cost as much as retraining. Break-even is the design target rather than a weakness. At that price the query bill alone equals the cost of training an equivalent model. The extractor still pays for the surrogate’s own training run and engineering on top of it while receiving a copy that the shaped outputs leave less faithful. Under the assumed equal-quality comparison, a lifetime price at or above break-even therefore removes the cost advantage of extraction over training an equivalent model independently. The residual route is to spread queries across many accounts, which account issuance controls and cross-account detection must bound, because a per-principal budget constrains an adversary only as far as principals map to real actors. The accuracy, latency, and false-positive figures are assumptions that the operator must measure before the design ships.

Pay-as-you-go pricing alone would charge the full training cost, but an extractor can stay inside the flat-fee tier, and tracking the cumulative bill against the queries collected shows what that choice is worth (figure 6). A daily quota stretches collection over 500 days but leaves the total near $833. A lifetime budget that bills every query beyond an allowance of 100K queries at the pay-as-you-go price instead makes the bill climb with the extraction set itself, reaching about $4,917 when the set is complete, close to the cost of training the model.

13.5.2 Leakage through authorized outputs

Whereas model theft copies the model, a second confidentiality failure needs no copy at all, because a model that executes correctly can disclose its training data through the outputs it is authorized to return. Persistent learning (section 13.1) carries sensitive information past the original processing, and the attacker reads nothing but permitted predictions, so storage encryption and caller authentication offer no protection. Three attacks exploit that leakage at increasing levels of detail. Membership inference learns a single bit indicating whether a given record was in the training set. Model inversion reconstructs properties of the training data, such as a representative input for a class or an identity. Training-data extraction recovers memorized records verbatim. All three need only query access or released weights, and all three grow more effective as the model fits its training data more closely than the population that data came from.

Membership inference

Membership inference tests whether a particular record was part of a model’s training set (Shokri et al. 2017). The attack exploits a gap that training creates. The model has fitted its training members, so it usually assigns them lower loss and higher confidence than records it has never seen. The simplest test thresholds that signal and declares a record a member when the model’s confidence on its true label exceeds a calibrated cutoff. A stronger test trains shadow models on data drawn from the same distribution with known membership. It learns from their outputs how member and nonmember responses differ, and it applies that classifier to the target model’s outputs (Shokri et al. 2017). Both tests succeed in proportion to the gap between training and held-out behavior, so the risk grows with overfitting and tends to concentrate on small datasets and on rare records that the model had to fit individually. A control added for another threat can widen that gap,5 so each one is rechecked against membership inference.

Shokri, Reza, Marco Stronati, Congzheng Song, and Vitaly Shmatikov. 2017. “Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models.” 2017 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 3–18. https://doi.org/10.1109/SP.2017.41.

5 Robustness-privacy trade-off: Adversarial training can increase susceptibility to membership inference in the settings studied by Song et al. (2019). The result means that a robustness intervention must be reevaluated against privacy invariants rather than assumed to improve every security property at once.

Song, Liwei, Reza Shokri, and Prateek Mittal. 2019. “Privacy Risks of Securing Machine Learning Models Against Adversarial Examples.” Proceedings of the 2019 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, 241–57. https://doi.org/10.1145/3319535.3354211.
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 2003. “Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule.”

For threat modeling, the relevant variable is what the adversary observes: confidence scores, labels only, or individual client updates. Attack success depends on the target model, data, outputs, and adversary knowledge. Confirming that an individual’s data was in a training set can still create privacy and compliance risk. In healthcare or legal prediction, membership itself can disclose sensitive information about a person, such as a diagnosis or a case. Whether that disclosure violates GDPR, HIPAA, or another rule depends on the data, parties, and deployment context (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2003).

Membership inference is also the standard privacy audit, and the audit and differential privacy bound the same leakage from opposite sides. An audit runs the strongest available attack against the trained model and reports its success. It must state which attacker access it assumes, because some threat models permit only model queries while others grant parameters or auxiliary information. A successful attack proves leakage. A failed attack shows only that this attack, under these assumptions, found none, so an empirical audit is a lower bound on what the model reveals. Differential privacy (section 13.9) supplies the upper bound. A membership test is itself a computation on the released model, so the guarantee applies to its verdict directly and limits how much more often any test can flag a protected record when that record was in training than when it was absent. Under a guarantee with budget \(\PrivacyBudget\) and no additive slack, the rate at which a test flags true members can exceed the rate at which it falsely flags nonmembers by at most a factor of \(e^{\PrivacyBudget}\), which places a ceiling over every possible attack. The distance between the measured lower bound and the accounted upper bound is the uncertainty that a privacy claim carries, the band between the audit curve and the ceiling in figure 7.

Model inversion

Model inversion infers sensitive properties of the training data, or a representative input for a class or identity, from the learned model (Fredrikson et al. 2015). It can use either query access or exposed model internals. Confidence scores, for example, can guide a search for inputs that the model associates with a target identity or attribute. A reconstructed face may reveal recognizable features without reproducing an exact training photograph; the privacy claim must distinguish those outcomes. Gradient inversion applies the same idea to the updates that a federated client sends (section 13.8.5.2).

Fredrikson, Matt, Somesh Jha, and Thomas Ristenpart. 2015. “Model Inversion Attacks That Exploit Confidence Information and Basic Countermeasures.” Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, 1322–33. https://doi.org/10.1145/2810103.2813677.

Memorization and training-data extraction

Memorization is the strongest form of the leak, in which a model retains enough of a specific training record to reproduce it. It is not confined to language models. Under one published extraction protocol, a diffusion model reproduced a training-set photograph almost exactly (Carlini et al. 2023); figure 8 pairs the original with the reconstruction. Evidence of extraction concerns that specific training instance; a similar-looking output of the same subject would not establish memorization. The exposure matters most for assistants trained or adapted on user logs, where the memorized strings are the users’ own messages.

GPT-2 data extraction case study

The GPT-2 extraction case shows why storage access control is insufficient once a model has learned sensitive content. In 2020, researchers demonstrated that query access to OpenAI’s GPT-2 model could reveal verbatim training examples (Carlini et al. 2021). The attack targeted information exposed through generation rather than direct access to the stored training dataset. The researchers generated hundreds of thousands of samples, some unconditioned and some seeded with short snippets of internet text. They then ranked the samples by how much more likely GPT-2 found them than a reference model or compression baseline did. This allowed them to extract personal information such as names, phone numbers, and email addresses, along with source code, unique identifiers, and other verbatim snippets that the model had memorized from its training data.

The technical approach exploited GPT-2’s memorization of rare or repeated text sequences through three stages. Sampling came first. The researchers generated 600,000 samples using top-\(\Glyph{k}\) sampling, sampling with a temperature that decays over the first generated tokens, and sampling conditioned on short prefixes drawn from internet text. Ranking then applied membership-inference metrics that compare GPT-2’s perplexity on a sample against a reference, namely the sample’s zlib compression entropy, the perplexity a smaller GPT-2 model assigns it, and GPT-2’s perplexity on the lowercased text. A sample that GPT-2 finds far more likely than the reference suggests memorization rather than fluent generalization. Manual verification closed the pipeline. The researchers inspected 1,800 top-ranked candidates, checking them first by internet search and then against the training data with OpenAI’s cooperation, and confirmed 604 of them as unique memorized training examples.

The attack challenged the assumption that training data would be “forgotten” after optimization. Some training examples remained recoverable even though the model was designed to generate text rather than retrieve records. Across the GPT-2 family studied (124M to 1.5B parameters), larger models exposed more memorized training data under the evaluation. This comparison motivates testing memorization as models scale; it does not establish a universal relationship between parameter count and privacy loss across different datasets and training procedures. For Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the deployment must therefore assess its actual corpus, training procedure, and exposed outputs rather than infer leakage from parameter count alone.

Filtering, deduplication, and manual review can reduce exposure, and output filters can screen known sensitive patterns, but empirical screening does not prove that no sensitive string remains recoverable. Differential privacy addresses a different requirement by bounding how much a protected contribution changes the distribution of released results. It does not prohibit every reproduction of text that appears in training, especially information shared across many records. Its contribution bound and the utility effects of filtering or private training must therefore be evaluated separately.

The result demonstrates why training-data controls need layered mitigations rather than storage access control alone (Carlini et al. 2021). Those layers can include filtering of personally identifiable information (PII), deduplication, extraction-style memorization audits, membership-inference testing, and differential privacy when a formal bound is required. Machine unlearning and policy controls address related lifecycle questions, but their guarantees require separate evidence and validation.

13.5.3 Data poisoning

While model theft and output leakage compromise confidentiality through read access to a finished model, data poisoning compromises training integrity through write access to something the model will learn from, arriving earlier in the lifecycle than any serving control can act. Injecting a few hundred mislabeled or trigger-stamped examples into a web-scraped corpus or user-feedback stream can plant a targeted backdoor while overall validation accuracy looks completely normal (Biggio et al. 2012).

Definition 13.4: Data poisoning

Data poisoning is the corruption of training data to compromise model behavior at inference time, either by injecting malicious samples or modifying existing labels.

  1. Significance: It undermines the foundational assumption of data integrity. Even a small fraction of poisoned samples can create backdoors or systematic biases that remain latent until triggered by specific inputs during serving.
  2. Distinction: Unlike inference-time evasion attacks against a fixed model, data poisoning operates through data collection or training, contaminating the model’s learned mapping from the source.
  3. Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that poisoning can be “fixed” by more data. In reality, poisoning often exploits the aggregation property of training: adding more clean data may not “wash out” a carefully targeted backdoor that uses a unique trigger.

Poisoned data may cause a model to make incorrect predictions, degrade its generalization ability, or embed failure modes that remain dormant until triggered after deployment. The exposure is greatest in applications that retrain on data collected from external sources, including user interactions, crowdsourced annotations, and online scraping, because an attacker can then contribute training data without any access to the training pipeline itself.

The access axes of section 13.4.1.2 apply with one change of emphasis. Model visibility still determines how precisely a poison can be crafted. A white-box attacker can optimize examples against the actual architecture and training procedure, while a black-box attacker relies on surrogates and open submission channels. What makes poisoning possible at all, however, is the write capability that the threat-vector scenarios separated from visibility. That capability can sit at collection, preprocessing, labeling, or storage, so the poisoning surface spans the whole data path. Its priority relative to other threats follows the deployment context analyzed in section 13.4.2.

A poisoning attempt spans admission, learning, and exploitation. The attacker first places manipulated examples where the training pipeline may accept them. Training then determines whether those examples induce the intended behavior; merely inserting a record does not guarantee success. If the altered behavior survives evaluation and deployment, the adversary may exploit it to cause selected errors or degrade service. The attack must therefore be evaluated through the actual learning procedure and release gates.

Data poisoning can be viewed as a bilevel optimization problem, because the attacker’s choice affects a model through the defender’s training procedure. In the outer problem, the attacker selects poisoning data \(\PoisoningDataset\) to increase loss on a validation or target dataset \(\PoisoningTargetDataset\). The inner problem trains the model on the resulting data. Let \(\CleanTrainingDataset\) represent the original training data. Subject to the attacker’s permitted modifications and poisoning budget, an untargeted objective is:

\[ \max_{\PoisoningDataset} \ \LossFunction(\PoisonedModel, \PoisoningTargetDataset) \tag{1}\]

where \(\PoisonedModel\) represents the model trained on the combined dataset of original and poisoned data. For targeted attacks, this objective can be refined to focus on specific inputs \(\ModelInput_t\) and target labels \(\ExampleLabel_t\): \[ \min_{\PoisoningDataset} \ \LossFunction(\PoisonedModel, \ModelInput_t, \ExampleLabel_t) \tag{2}\]

In the training system, the nested objectives become two coupled loops (figure 9). The outer loop is the attacker’s proposal step, which optimizes the attack objective, either raising loss on the test set (equation 1) or, for a targeted attack, lowering loss on the chosen label \(\ExampleLabel_t\) (equation 2). The inner loop is the defender’s training process, which minimizes loss on the combined data. The attacker evaluates or approximates this inner effect on training, and uses the resulting target loss to refine the proposal. An attacker without access to the defender’s training process must instead rely on a surrogate or other available feedback.

This formulation captures the adversary’s goal of introducing carefully crafted data points to manipulate the model’s decision boundaries. Consider an email spam filter that retrains on messages users report as legitimate. An attacker who controls a set of accounts can report a batch of messages written in the style of an upcoming campaign as “not spam.” The goal is to shift the filter’s decision boundary so that the campaign’s future messages reach inboxes. In this case, the poisoning data \(\PoisoningDataset\) consists of mislabeled campaign-style messages, and the attacker’s objective is to have the campaign messages \(\ModelInput_t\) classified as legitimate mail \(\ExampleLabel_t\), following the targeted attack formulation in equation 2. If the mislabeled messages influence training enough to induce that behavior, aggregate performance on other traffic may still appear normal. The contrast with the stop-sign stickers that opened the discussion of model-specific attacks is the lifecycle stage. Poisoning changes the model before deployment, whereas the stickers change only the input that an unmodified deployed model receives.

Data poisoning attacks differ in their objective and scope (Biggio et al. 2012). Availability attacks seek broad degradation of useful performance. Targeted attacks seek errors on selected inputs or classes and may leave aggregate accuracy largely unchanged (Shafahi et al. 2018). Backdoor attacks associate an attacker-chosen trigger with unwanted behavior; the trigger can be visible, as in a sticker, even when its significance is hidden (Gu et al. 2017). Subpopulation attacks instead target a group defined by shared features (Jagielski et al. 2021). These categories can overlap. Their objectives guide which evaluations are needed beyond aggregate accuracy, including targeted, trigger-specific, and subgroup tests.

Biggio, Battista, Blaine Nelson, and Pavel Laskov. 2012. “Poisoning Attacks Against Support Vector Machines.” Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2012, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK, June 26 - July 1, 2012.
Jagielski, Matthew, Giorgio Severi, Niklas Pousette Harger, and Alina Oprea. 2021. “Subpopulation Data Poisoning Attacks.” Proceedings of the 2021 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, 3104–22. https://doi.org/10.1145/3460120.3485368.

The objective classes say what an attacker wants; the attack mechanism depends on the attacker’s access to the system and knowledge of the data pipeline. Every mechanism shares the shape traced in figure 10, in which a poisoned record enters the training pipeline alongside clean data and attempts to alter the resulting model’s behavior. The most direct mechanism is label modification, where an attacker selects a subset of training samples and alters their labels, flipping \(\ExampleLabel= 1\) to \(\ExampleLabel= 0\) or reassigning categories in multi-class settings. Even small-scale label corruption can shift decision boundaries. At web scale the same mechanism mislabels multimodal pretraining pairs, as in the dirty-label sample of figure 11, which pairs cat images with misleading “dog” captions to induce false associations.

Beyond label modification, the attacker can keep the label intact and corrupt the features instead, the strategy known as clean-label poisoning. Because every label is correct, label audits cannot flag these records. Imperceptible image perturbations, subtle shifts in structured fields, and fixed trigger patterns aim for the same outcome. In each case the training example still appears legitimate, but it bends the learned decision boundary toward a future failure. Generative methods and data-synthesis tools raise the same risk at larger scale because they can create natural-looking examples whose only purpose is to distort what the model learns.

Clean-label poisoning is not always malicious in intent; researchers have begun exploring it as a defensive tool, particularly for protecting creative work from unauthorized use by generative AI models. Nightshade, developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, aims to deter unauthorized training by poisoning images that a scraper may collect (Shan et al. 2023). It does not block scraping itself. Its perturbations preserve the apparent image content while changing how a model learns from it; the reported experiments show targeted concept corruption when the modified images enter the tested training pipelines.

The dose-response matrix in figure 12 charts this progressive corruption across four poison doses (0 to 300 samples) and eight prompt concepts. As the dose increases, Stable Diffusion XL outputs morph away from source concepts (generating cows for “car” or cats for “dog”) under the tested training conditions. These outputs demonstrate changed behavior without, by themselves, identifying the internal representation that caused it. The experiment demonstrates concept poisoning, in which poisoned samples distort a model’s semantic associations.

The Nightshade experiments also report effects on concepts related to the poisoned target. This spillover extends the observed attack beyond the exact target prompt, but its reach depends on the model, poison construction, and training procedure. The same technique used to protect artistic content could also be repurposed to sabotage legitimate training pipelines, highlighting the dual-use dilemma6 at the heart of machine learning security.

6 Dual-use dilemma: The structural tension that defensive ML capabilities (adversarial training, data poisoning tools, red-teaming frameworks) are simultaneously offensive capabilities. This creates an arms race where defensive research publications become attack playbooks. For ML systems engineering, the consequence is architectural: robustness mechanisms must assume attacker knowledge of the defense, ruling out security-through-obscurity and motivating formal guarantees where feasible and adaptive empirical evaluation within the remaining threat model.

Whether crafted examples become poisoning depends on the data boundary. Web scraping, social media feeds, crowdsourced annotation, and untrusted user submissions all allow poisoned records to enter upstream and pass through weak cleaning checks in a “trusted” form. Physical systems add a second path. A sticker on a road sign is an inference-time adversarial attack when the car sees it, but an image of it harvested into a training corpus becomes a poisoning path only if the contribution serves an attack on the learner. Correctly labeled examples of such inputs can instead help train resistance to them. Online learning systems tighten the feedback loop further, allowing an attacker to introduce small increments of malicious data until model behavior drifts without a single obvious anomaly. In collaborative training the same boundary sits at aggregation, where one malicious client’s update reaches every participant (figure 13). Section 13.6.1 examines the same exposure among the workers of a synchronous data-parallel job.

Mitigating poisoning requires controls from data admission through model evaluation, and Data Poisoning Defenses develops those defenses and the evidence for them. Because targeted and backdoor attacks can preserve aggregate validation accuracy, clean evaluation cannot certify integrity. The provenance bound on trust (principle 22) makes source verification and lineage necessary evidence about what entered training, but a verified source can still supply harmful records. Validation and anomaly detection examine those records, while robust training can limit their influence under a specified contamination model. Release evaluation must then test the targeted behaviors that ordinary accuracy metrics can miss.

↪ Poisoning defenses, from data sanitization to robust training, are developed in Data Poisoning Defenses.

13.5.4 Adversarial attacks

An attacker who can modify a sensor input or submit an API request can target the deployed model without changing its training data. The security question is which inputs the actor can control and which service decisions those inputs can influence. Behavioral robustness asks how much the model’s predictions degrade under that specified manipulation. Here the threat model establishes the allowed attack; Adversarial Defenses develops the evaluation and training methods needed to measure and improve resistance.

Adversarial inputs exploit the deployed model’s decision behavior under attacker-chosen modifications. Some attacks use small, hard-to-perceive perturbations; others use visible patches or changes allowed by a physical or semantic constraint. The threat model must state those constraints before attack success or defense quality can be measured. This shifts attention from the integrity of upstream training data to the inputs and decisions exposed during inference.

These attacks create real-world risks in domains such as autonomous driving, biometric authentication, and content moderation. Small, visually hard-to-distinguish perturbations can cause image classifiers to make high-confidence errors (Szegedy et al. 2013; Goodfellow et al. 2015). Physical-world work showed that printed adversarial images can survive camera capture and remain misclassified by an ImageNet classifier (Kurakin et al. 2017). Road-sign attacks then showed that small stickers or perturbations can cause signs to be misclassified under realistic viewing conditions (Eykholt et al. 2018). A deployed defense must be evaluated against attacks adapted to its mechanisms. Changing the attacker model or the deployment can invalidate earlier evidence, so each change requires renewed testing.

Kurakin, Alexey, Ian Goodfellow, and Samy Bengio. 2017. “Adversarial Examples in the Physical World.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), Workshop Track, 99–112. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781351251389-8.
Eykholt, K., I. Evtimov, E. Fernandes, B. Li, A. Rahmati, C. Xiao, A. Prakash, T. Kohno, and D. Song. 2018. “Robust Physical-World Attacks on Deep Learning Visual Classification.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 1707.08945: 1625–34. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00175.

7 Perspective API: Google’s toxicity model has been reported in use across many platforms, including The New York Times and Wikipedia. A shared classifier can create correlated exposure to an evasion technique, but success at each site also depends on its model version, preprocessing, thresholds, and additional moderation controls.

Hosseini, Hossein, Sreeram Kannan, Baosen Zhang, and Radha Poovendran. 2017. “Deceiving Google’s Perspective API Built for Detecting Toxic Comments.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1702.08138, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1702.08138.

The Perspective API case makes the inference-time distinction concrete. Researchers studying Google’s toxicity detection API in 20177 showed that subtle misspellings, character substitutions, and added punctuation could cause explicitly toxic phrases to receive low toxicity scores (Hosseini et al. 2017). The training pipeline had not been poisoned; the deployed decision surface was fragile to small input perturbations.

The shared abstraction is a search over permitted input changes for an outcome the attacker wants. A norm bound constrains numerical distance, while a physical constraint may limit sticker placement or camera conditions. Neither automatically establishes that a modification is imperceptible or harmless to a human observer.

The access types of section 13.4.1.2 determine how that search proceeds. White-box access lets the attacker compute input gradients directly, while black-box and gray-box attackers must estimate them from queries, partial architecture knowledge, or a surrogate model. Common attack strategies include surrogate model construction, transfer attacks exploiting adversarial transferability8 (Papernot et al. 2016), and generative adversarial network (GAN)-based perturbation generation. The evaluation must also state the query budget and which inputs the actor can modify.

8 Adversarial transferability: Adversarial inputs crafted on one model can also fool another (Szegedy et al. 2013; Papernot et al. 2016). A surrogate can therefore support an attack without target-model parameters, but transfer success depends on the models, data, and allowed perturbations; it is not uniformly comparable to white-box access.

Szegedy, Christian, Wojciech Zaremba, Ilya Sutskever, Joan Bruna, Dumitru Erhan, Ian Goodfellow, and Rob Fergus. 2013. “Intriguing Properties of Neural Networks.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1312.6199.
Papernot, Nicolas, Patrick McDaniel, and Ian Goodfellow. 2016. “Transferability in Machine Learning: From Phenomena to Black-Box Attacks Using Adversarial Samples.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1605.07277.

↪ Gradient-based perturbation attacks and their white-box, black-box, and transfer variants are developed in Adversarial Attacks.

Madry, Aleksander, Aleksandar Makelov, Ludwig Schmidt, Dimitris Tsipras, and Adrian Vladu. 2018. “Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Because these attacks succeed against models with high clean accuracy, defenses must act on the attack itself. They divide between runtime controls, such as input validation and anomaly monitoring during inference (section 13.8.3), and training-time methods such as adversarial training on deliberately perturbed examples (Madry et al. 2018). Adversarial Defenses evaluates both against stated threat models.

The threat model usually bounds the attacker’s change to a ball around the clean input, \(\|\AdversarialPerturbation\| \leq \AdversarialPerturbationBudget\). A perturbation inside that radius succeeds when it carries the input across a decision boundary. The radius \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\) lives in input space and is unrelated to the privacy budget \(\PrivacyBudget\) of section 13.9. The stop-sign stickers that opened the discussion of model-specific attacks are the physical form of such a boundary crossing. Physical-world attacks treats the case as a robustness problem and examines what its separate laboratory and field-test success rates imply for evaluation.

13.5.5 LLM-specific attack vectors

The same inference-time framing extends to large language models (LLMs), where security surveys catalog prompt injection, jailbreaking, data leakage, and malicious reuse as cybersecurity and privacy risks (Gupta et al. 2023). The systems mechanism is that the interface often mixes instructions, user content, retrieved context, and policy controls in one token stream, making the boundary between control and data fragile (Perez and Ribeiro 2022). The boundary is weakest where retrieved or external content enters that stream, because text the system fetched can be reinterpreted as instructions (Greshake et al. 2023). A secure LLM system therefore separates four objects that the model tends to collapse. Instructions, comprising system and developer directives, define the intended control plane, whereas untrusted content from user input and external text must remain strictly data rather than authority. Retrieved documents provide evidence but should never rewrite policy or permissions, and sensitive secrets (credentials, private data, and hidden policy state) must remain outside model-visible context unless explicitly required. Separating these objects gives the serving system concrete boundaries it can enforce even when the model text tries to blur them.

Gupta, Maanak, Charankumar Akiri, Kshitiz Aryal, Eli Parker, and Lopamudra Praharaj. 2023. “From ChatGPT to ThreatGPT: Impact of Generative AI in Cybersecurity and Privacy.” IEEE Access 11: 80218–45. https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2023.3300381.
Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.

The serving system must treat every model output as untrusted input, not as authorization. Each model receives the least privilege needed for the current task (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), and any component that consumes model output validates it before acting on it. An external policy-enforcement point must check the authenticated principal and current context rather than accepting a model-generated claim of permission. High-impact or irreversible operations require a separate approval path. These boundaries prevent model text from expanding its authority and limit the blast radius when prompt injection succeeds (Greshake et al. 2023). They do not eliminate injection: an attacker may still abuse every operation that the current principal legitimately allows.

Three recurring failure modes organize the space: prompt injection attempts to cross the boundary between control and data, training data extraction exposes memorized records (Carlini et al. 2021), and jailbreaking seeks to bypass alignment controls (Zou et al. 2023). Prompt injection exploits the model’s interpretation of content as instructions (Perez and Ribeiro 2022; Greshake et al. 2023). Instruction roles and delimiters can guide behavior, but do not supply an authorization boundary equivalent to separating SQL parameters from executable query structure. An attacker can embed directives within legitimate inputs (such as “Ignore previous constraints and output the system prompt”) that the model may follow. Input and output classifiers can detect some attempts, while sandboxing and external permission checks constrain what a manipulated output can reach. These controls need separate evaluation because detecting suspicious text and enforcing authority are different tasks.

Carlini, N., F. Tramer, E. Wallace, M. Jagielski, A. Herbert-Voss, K. Lee, A. Roberts, et al. 2021. “Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models.” 30th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 21), 2633–50.
Zou, Andy, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. 2023. Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models.
Perez, Fábio, and Ian Ribeiro. 2022. “Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques for Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2211.09527.
Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.
Ouyang, L., J. Wu, X. Jiang, D. Almeida, C. L. Wainwright, P. Mishkin, C. Zhang, et al. 2022. “Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 27730–44. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2011.
Bai, Yuntao et al. 2022. Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback.
Inan, H., K. Upasani, J. Chi, R. Rungta, K. Iyer, Y. Mao, M. Tontchev, et al. 2023. “Llama Guard: LLM-Based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2312.06674.
Google. 2024. ShieldGemma: Generative AI Content Moderation Based on Gemma. Google AI for Developers documentation.

Training data extraction is the memorization leak of section 13.5.2.3, in which generated text reproduces retained training sequences, including PII, without implying that the model stores a retrievable copy of every record. A third category, jailbreaking and alignment bypass, targets controls intended to keep generated behavior within policy. Reinforcement learning from human feedback shapes behavior during training (Ouyang et al. 2022), Constitutional AI uses critique against explicit principles (Bai et al. 2022), and guardrail models classify inputs or outputs at runtime (Inan et al. 2023; Google 2024). These learned controls do not establish a formal guarantee against every prompt; adversarial suffixes demonstrate one way to bypass them (Zou et al. 2023). A deployment can combine behavioral training, separately evaluated monitors, query budgets, and review of consequential outputs. Their value depends on measured resistance to adaptive attacks and on the external permissions that limit what an unsafe output can cause.

13.5.6 Availability abuse and denial of wallet

Generative serving also exposes availability to an attack that needs no flood of requests. The cost of a request grows with the tokens it generates and the documents it retrieves, so an attacker can select requests that maximize that work or defeat cache reuse, consuming more accelerator time and downstream service capacity than ordinary traffic while the endpoint remains reachable. In this denial-of-wallet scenario, the attacker targets the cost budget rather than only the request queue: autoscaling (Autoscaling and Capacity Control) can preserve apparent availability by purchasing more capacity while spend and tail latency exceed their operating limits.

Availability defenses must therefore meter work, not merely request counts. The mechanisms are the overload controls that already protect a serving fleet; what security changes is the signal they act on, which becomes work and cost per authenticated principal rather than aggregate load. The serving boundary should assign budgets to input size, generated tokens, retrieval calls, concurrent work, and cumulative cost per authenticated principal. Admission control can reject or degrade requests before they reserve scarce accelerators; bounded generation, timeouts, circuit breakers, and per-request retrieval quotas limit the work admitted by any one request. Operators should monitor cost per successful result alongside latency and error rate because an attacker can preserve HTTP success while exhausting the service’s economic budget. These controls also constrain model extraction, but their availability objective is distinct. They keep adversarially induced work from displacing legitimate service or producing unbounded spend.

↩︎ Circuit breakers and backpressure, the serving fleet’s overload controls, are established in Circuit breakers and backpressure.

While LLM control-data entanglement cuts across multiple objectives inside a single token stream, the five primary lifecycle objectives span distinct stages of the ML pipeline and demand targeted defensive strategies. Grouping those five objectives by lifecycle stage and attack vector (table 5) shows where each vulnerability appears and which mitigation it calls for.

The appropriate defense depends on the attack vector, lifecycle stage, and available evidence. For each threat, assessment evidence and candidate controls play different roles (figure 14). Monitoring can reveal suspicious querying, while watermarking can support attribution after extraction; neither establishes that theft was prevented. Privacy audits measure attack success under tested conditions, whereas an accounted DP mechanism provides a formal bound under its stated assumptions. Each row identifies a design starting point, not a guaranteed detection-to-defense pipeline, and this distinction between training-time and inference-time attacks is easiest to verify in a concrete deployment scenario.

Checkpoint 13.2: Knowledge check: Model attacks

An autonomous vehicle’s vision system misclassifies a stop sign as a speed limit sign because of a specially crafted sticker placed on the sign. This attack happens at inference time without access to the training data.

Model theft, output leakage, poisoning, and adversarial inputs all reach the model through an interface the fleet exposes on purpose: a query endpoint, a data feed, or a sensor. A fleet also has interfaces it never exposes to users, between its own workers, tenants, and nodes, and those interfaces carry the next set of threats.

Self-Check: Question

  1. A security architect must deploy defenses against two distinct model theft vectors: (1) an unauthorized party copying serialized model checkpoints from a cloud bucket, and (2) a competitor sending millions of synthetic queries to a public REST endpoint to distill a student model. Which combination of defenses correctly targets each vector?

    1. Vector (1) requires output rounding and top-\(k\) truncation; Vector (2) requires hardware security modules for model weights at rest.
    2. Vector (1) requires differential privacy during training; Vector (2) requires air-gapping the inference server from the internet.
    3. Vector (1) requires encrypted storage, signed model artifacts, and strict IAM/RBAC permissions; Vector (2) requires rate limiting, query anomaly monitoring, and confidence-score truncation.
    4. Both vectors are mitigated exclusively by converting model checkpoints to Python pickle files.

  2. Data poisoning is formalized as a bilevel optimization problem. State the attacker’s untargeted outer objective and the defender’s inner training objective, and explain why evaluating a poison’s learning effect can be computationally demanding.

  3. Research on language model APIs (e.g., Carlini et al., 2024) demonstrated that output-projection matrices of models like OpenAI ada and babbage could be extracted with root-mean-square errors around \(10^{-4}\) using fewer than \(4 \times 10^6\) queries at a cost of under $15. In an image API serving a 1,000-class classifier, what is the systems effect of replacing full softmax probability distributions with top-5 class predictions and rounding confidences to 2 decimal places?

    1. It completely eliminates all adversarial perturbation vectors while increasing inference latency by 100x.
    2. It introduces a formal \((\epsilon, \delta)\) differential privacy guarantee across all subsequent user queries.
    3. It reduces model parameter size in GPU VRAM by 99.5% during the forward pass.
    4. It returns 99.5% fewer distribution entries and coarser confidences; extraction resistance and legitimate-client utility require separate measurement.

  4. In the road-sign study, stickers on a stop sign changed only the input a deployed classifier received. Explain why a numerical perturbation norm alone does not establish physical feasibility or human recognizability, and what a physical threat model must state in addition.

  5. True or False: A model compromised by a backdoor attack (such as BadNets) will exhibit a noticeable drop in validation accuracy on standard, clean test datasets, allowing automated validation pipelines to flag the compromise before deployment.

  6. A team runs a shadow-model membership-inference audit against its model and finds attack accuracy barely above chance. Explain what this result establishes, what it does not, and what would supply a bound that holds against any membership test.

13.6 Fleet-Internal Trust Boundaries

A training job on the reference cluster of 1,024 GPUs (128 nodes with 8 GPUs each) depends on contributions from many participants. Each optimizer step of the Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) reference model reduces 350 GB of FP16 gradients across the job, and each checkpoint interval produces a 2.45 TB artifact containing valuable learned state. Public inference controls do not govern these internal exchanges. Four boundaries determine how a node compromise can propagate: the gradient each worker contributes, the fabric that carries it, the accelerators and caches tenants share, and the evidence used to admit nodes into the job.

13.6.1 Gradient synchronization integrity

Because standard ring AllReduce averages worker contributions with a breakdown point of zero, a single compromised node submitting an arbitrarily large gradient vector can corrupt the global step for all 1,024 GPUs. Weighting each of the \(\DataParallelDegree\) contributions by \(1/\DataParallelDegree\) does not bound that corruption when the contribution’s magnitude is unconstrained. Byzantine failures introduces aggregation rules such as Krum and coordinate-wise trimmed mean, whose guarantees require assumptions about the number of faulty workers and the honest updates (Blanchard et al. 2017; Yin et al. 2018). An intentional adversary can adapt its update to the deployed norm or distance checks and repeat the attempt across steps. Evaluation must therefore test attacks against the active control rather than rely only on evidence from random faults.

Blanchard, Peva, El Mahdi El Mhamdi, Rachid Guerraoui, and Julien Stainer. 2017. “Machine Learning with Adversaries: Byzantine Tolerant Gradient Descent.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 119–29.
Yin, Dong, Yudong Chen, Kannan Ramchandran, and Peter Bartlett. 2018. “Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning: Towards Optimal Statistical Rates.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 5650–59.

Robust aggregation also changes the collective’s information requirements. Ring AllReduce computes a sum with about \(2(\DataParallelDegree-1)/\DataParallelDegree\) times the gradient size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) in per-worker communication as \(\DataParallelDegree\) grows; its result does not provide a separate gradient for every worker. A direct implementation of a median, trimmed mean, or distance-based rule can instead gather all individual gradients. Gathering them at every worker receives \((\DataParallelDegree-1)\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes per worker, a factor of \(\DataParallelDegree/2\) relative to the ring traffic expression. Unlike the device count \(\DeviceCount\) of the Fleet Law, the \(\DataParallelDegree\) here is the data-parallel degree, which counts model replicas rather than accelerators. The comparison assumes a data-parallel degree of 64 on the reference cluster, which leaves each replica two full nodes of 8 GPUs (for example, tensor parallelism inside each node). At that degree \(\DataParallelDegree/2\) gives 32× the ring traffic. Because the gradient synchronization is bandwidth-dominated, its share of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) grows by roughly that factor unless the extra traffic can be overlapped with backward computation. That ratio is the cost of the gather-based implementation, not a lower bound for every robust protocol. Worker admission through attestation (section 13.6.4) restricts which environments join the job, but does not prove their gradients are benign; update checks or redundant computation address different evidence. Federated deployments face heterogeneous attestation support and independently controlled clients. Federated privacy examines the additional conflict between inspecting individual updates and hiding them through secure aggregation.

↩︎ Ring AllReduce and its \(2(\DataParallelDegree-1)/\DataParallelDegree\) per-worker traffic bound are established in Ring AllReduce.

13.6.2 Collective traffic confidentiality

Moving 350 GB of plaintext FP16 gradients per step over remote direct memory access (RDMA) bypasses host CPUs for speed, but exposes sensitive training updates to any adversary who can tap the fabric links, switches, or management plane. Gradient inversion, examined for federated clients in section 13.8.5.2, demonstrates that exposed gradients can reconstruct training examples under particular observation and training conditions. The exposure of a gradient shard, aggregate, or activation therefore needs its own analysis of what an observer on the fabric can recover. A dedicated facility can restrict physical access to links and switches without eliminating the fabric trust boundary.

↩︎ RDMA and GPUDirect transports, which move payloads directly between accelerator memories, are established in RDMA and GPUDirect.

Encrypting collective traffic can add to the communication term of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3). The size of that addition follows from the ring traffic just derived. For the large gradient buckets that dominate a step, the bandwidth term of the AllReduce, about \(2(\DataParallelDegree-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/(\DataParallelDegree\LinkBandwidth)\) for link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), outweighs the per-message latency. A cipher that sustains only half the link rate therefore halves the effective \(\LinkBandwidth\) and roughly doubles that part of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\). A cipher that keeps pace with the link adds latency but little transfer time, while a host-based path that stages accelerator data adds copies that GPUDirect RDMA avoids. Adapter or link-layer encryption can protect traffic without that staging path, subject to the endpoints and keys included in its trust boundary.
