The added latency and any lost overlap must be measured on the actual collective schedule, because repeated increases in \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) affect the capacity required for the run.

13.6.3 Shared accelerators and caches

Sharing a GPU across tenants without hardware memory partitioning or prefix-cache scoping lets one tenant infer another’s prompt prefix from response-timing hits or read residual high-bandwidth memory (HBM) state. When a serving engine shares its key-value prefix cache across tenants, a request whose opening tokens match a cached prefix skips prefill computation and returns its first token noticeably faster, letting a co-tenant probe whether a target system prompt or document was recently processed. At the processor layer, Volta-era and later Multi-Process Service implementations provide separate client GPU address spaces, but processes still share compute units, caches, and memory controllers without hardware fault isolation, so address separation alone does not establish a boundary between mutually distrustful users. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions memory, cache, and compute resources in hardware (NVIDIA 2026), while sequential reuse introduces a separate requirement to scrub accessible residual memory before reassignment. Tenant-scoped prefix caches remove cross-tenant timing leakage at a potential hit-rate cost, leaving other timing channels and within-tenant access boundaries to be assessed.

NVIDIA. 2026. NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU User Guide.

↩︎ The accelerator sharing options and the isolation strength each provides are established in Resource isolation.

Each of these controls spends capacity, through reserved partitions, fragmentation, scrubbing time, or lost cache reuse. Measuring that capacity effect requires a matched workload and resource budget; a smaller partition cannot be compared with a whole accelerator and labeled pure security overhead.

Systems Perspective 13.2: The cost of secure multi-tenancy
Consider a hypothetical comparison of two serving configurations with the same allocated accelerator capacity, models, request mix, and latency target. Assume the baseline sustains 1,000 tokens per second and the configuration with additional security controls sustains 850 tokens per second. These are scenario inputs for a capacity calculation, not measured overheads for MIG or another isolation mechanism.

For this matched comparison, the throughput loss is 1,000 tokens - 850 tokens = 150 tokens per second, or (150 tokens/1,000 tokens) = 15 percent. Spatial partitioning does not inherently require tenant context switches. Its capacity cost may instead arise from fragmentation or idle reserved resources, which should be recorded separately from execution overhead.

Systems insight: The assumed controls reduce useful throughput by 15 percent under the stated comparison. In a measured deployment that loss would split among the mechanisms of this section. Hardware partitions strand capacity whenever a tenant’s load falls below its slice, memory scrubbing between tenants takes time out of every reassignment, and tenant-scoped prefix caches give up the hits that cross-tenant reuse would have supplied. Each source has a different remedy. Right-sizing partitions recovers stranded capacity, while cache scoping is the price of closing a timing channel and cannot be tuned away without reopening it. Fleet planning must therefore record each source separately; none can be inferred from comparing a whole accelerator with a smaller partition.

13.6.4 Attestation and key custody at fleet scale

When 128 cluster nodes restart and update independently, releasing the decryption key for a 2.45 TB checkpoint to a node whose boot firmware was silently modified exposes the entire model. Remote attestation lets a verifier appraise authenticated hardware claims about each node against an admission policy before delivering keys or data. The central claim is a set of measurements, cryptographic hashes of the firmware and software the node loaded, recorded and signed by the node’s hardware so that compromised software cannot rewrite them. Before releasing the key for the 2.45 TB checkpoint, the service can require fresh evidence covering the relevant firmware and workload measurements. Coverage depends on the platform; a valid measurement does not prove that approved code is free of vulnerabilities or that every runtime update is correct. The provenance bound on trust (principle 22) links this evidence to the release path. Confidential computing adds runtime protection for code and data placed inside a hardware-enforced boundary, under the platform’s stated adversary model. Section 13.8.1 develops those mechanisms and their limits.

The recovery sequence in figure 15 places key delivery between fresh appraisal and checkpoint restoration.

Attestation and key management add coordination work when admission or recovery requires renewed evidence and key delivery. The policy must specify when evidence expires and which changes require another check. Key rotation also needs a transition plan, while revocation after a suspected compromise may require interrupting work that no longer has valid authority. Hardware security modules can protect the keys used to authorize or wrap secrets, with node-level custody governed separately. When these operations delay participants or restart, their cost enters \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and the recovery path. A node that restarts after a failure must present fresh evidence and receive the checkpoint key again before it rejoins, so every failure costs that re-admission delay on top of the restart time and lost work that the checkpoint-interval calculation already charges.

↩︎ The Young-Daly checkpoint interval, which balances checkpoint write cost against expected lost work, is established in The Young-Daly checkpoint interval.

The four boundaries draw on all three C³ axes. Redundant computation and memory scrubbing add compute work, while tenant-scoped caches can reduce reuse. Robust aggregation and encrypted collectives can add communication cost; attestation and key rotation add coordination. These controls also depend on components beneath the job. A driver with access to plaintext state, a compromised memory path, or an observable power signal can undermine a protection enforced higher in the stack. The hardware threat model must identify which of those components remain trusted and which observations the attacker can obtain.

Self-Check: Question

  1. A 64-worker data-parallel job replaces ring AllReduce with a gather-based coordinate-wise median implementation: every worker gathers every individual gradient before computing the median. Approximately how does per-worker gradient traffic change under this schedule?

    1. It rises by about 32 times, because this implementation gathers the 63 peer gradients instead of moving about twice the gradient size in the ring.
    2. It is unchanged, because this median implementation uses only the sum returned by ring AllReduce.
    3. It roughly doubles, because gathering all individual gradients costs one extra ring pass.
    4. It falls, because the implementation discards outlier gradients before receiving them.

  2. Two hypothetical serving configurations use the same allocated accelerator capacity, models, request mix, and latency target. The baseline sustains 1,000 tokens/s and the configuration with additional security controls sustains 850 tokens/s. Explain what this 15% capacity loss establishes and why comparing a whole GPU against a smaller MIG partition would not isolate security overhead.

  3. True or False: RDMA movement between accelerator memories establishes gradient confidentiality even when the fabric payloads are plaintext.

  4. A multi-tenant LLM service shares one prefix cache across all tenants, and cache hits are distinguishable in time-to-first-token measurements. What can a probing tenant infer, and which control removes this cross-tenant cache-reuse path?

    1. Evidence that a probed prefix was recently processed outside the probing tenant; per-tenant cache scoping removes this shared-reuse path at the cost of a lower hit rate.
    2. The model weights of the serving replica; encrypting the weights at rest closes the channel.
    3. Another tenant’s API key; mutual TLS between client and gateway closes the channel.
    4. The exact output tokens of other tenants; rounding output probabilities closes the channel.

  5. When a 128-node training job waits for fresh remote attestation and key delivery before admission or recovery, explain why that delay enters the coordination term and recovery path of the Fleet Law. Distinguish it from steady-state protected-execution costs.

See Answers →

13.7 Hardware-Level Security Vulnerabilities

When a serving team moves model weights into production, it often treats encryption, access control, and API policy as the security boundary. Hardware attacks break that assumption. A processor can leak across isolation domains, a field device can be opened, a bus or power rail can expose signals, and a counterfeit component can enter the system before deployment begins. Hardware therefore belongs inside the threat model, as the substrate that can invalidate software controls after those controls appear to pass.

The practical deployment question is which substrate layer can still violate trust. A cloud LLM endpoint is mostly an isolation problem, because one tenant’s process, memory, and accelerator context must not reveal another tenant’s prompts or weights. An embedded vision sensor is mostly a physical-access problem, because the attacker may probe power, attach to a debug port, or replace a module. A regulated procurement pipeline is mostly a provenance problem, because the organization must know which components were built, handled, patched, and retired. These cases use different defenses, but they share the same reasoning pattern.

Hardware security planning therefore begins with four fundamental checks. Processor isolation must separate tenants, cryptographic keys, model weights, and intermediate activations from untrusted code and co-tenants. Physical-access controls must protect devices, sensors, memory, and debug interfaces when attackers can physically touch the hardware. Side-channel evaluation tests whether observable power, timing, electromagnetic, bus, or thermal signals expose sensitive computation despite those boundaries. Finally, supply-chain validation checks evidence that the deployed component matches the component the system was designed and certified to use. Each check needs an explicit attacker model; passing it does not establish protection against access or measurements outside that model.

Grouping the hardware threat landscape by these four checks rather than by attack family ties each vulnerability to the deployment decision that controls it (table 6). The defensive strategies in section 13.8 return to the same decisions from the perspective of trusted execution, attestation, and hardware roots of trust.

Each threat family tests one of those decisions. Hardware bugs test processor isolation. Physical attacks, fault injection, and leaky interfaces test whether direct access can change the system after software controls pass. Side-channel attacks test whether computation leaks through observable signals. Supply chain risks, from a single counterfeit part to a compromised part number, test whether the deployed component is the one the architecture assumes.

13.7.1 Hardware bugs

When tenants share a cloud host, a transient-execution flaw such as Spectre or Meltdown in the CPU can leak decrypted keys, prompts, or feature batches across process boundaries after software access checks have already passed (Lipp et al. 2018; Kocher et al. 2019). Hardware bugs therefore test the first deployment decision: whether processor isolation can be trusted as an empirical boundary rather than a default guarantee. Attackers can exploit these microarchitectural design flaws to bypass memory isolation and read the data of co-tenant applications and the operating system.

Lipp, M., M. Schwarz, D. Gruss, T. Prescher, W. Haas, J. Horn, S. Mangard, et al. 2018. “Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space.” Proceedings of the 27th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security), 973–90.
Kocher, Paul, Jann Horn, Anders Fogh, Daniel Genkin, Daniel Gruss, Werner Haas, Mike Hamburg, et al. 2019. “Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution.” 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 1–19. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2019.00002.

Spectre exploits speculative execution, a performance optimization in which a CPU executes instructions along a predicted path before it knows whether that path is correct. An attacker influences the prediction so that a victim transiently accesses sensitive data. Meltdown instead exploits affected processors that transiently make data available before enforcing the access restriction. In both cases, discarding the unauthorized or mispredicted computation can leave observable traces in microarchitectural state, such as CPU caches. Software-visible execution can therefore respect a boundary while the traces of transient execution leak across it.

Further research identified related transient-execution attacks, including Foreshadow, ZombieLoad, and RIDL, against different microarchitectural structures in affected processors. Their existence motivates examining each component’s isolation assumptions without assuming that every processor shares the same vulnerability. ML systems pair CPUs with GPUs, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), or custom accelerators. A compromise can propagate across this heterogeneous stack when components share sensitive data, keys, or privileged access; the threat model must trace those relationships.

For a fleet, the consequence can be cross-tenant exposure. Host processors stage data for accelerators, run tokenizers and preprocessing, and hold decrypted keys. When tenants share a vulnerable host and the required attack conditions hold, a transient-execution flaw can expose sensitive state before any accelerator is involved. Mitigations depend on the vulnerability and deployment: restricting simultaneous multithreading or clearing affected microarchitectural state at isolation boundaries can reduce throughput on the data-loading and serving paths that keep accelerators fed. The fleet must remeasure those paths after applying the relevant protections rather than assume a fixed overhead.

Hardware security therefore extends beyond physical tamper prevention to architectural isolation: preventing processors, accelerators, and memory systems from leaking across boundaries the software assumes are sealed. Mitigations often carry performance costs, especially for data-bound ML workloads, so confidential computing (section 13.6.4) and trusted execution environments (TEEs) must be evaluated as capacity and latency decisions as well as security decisions.

13.7.2 Physical attacks

An attacker who can physically touch an edge drone or biometric kiosk can swap a camera module, probe a memory bus, or attach to an unlocked debug port, bypassing every network firewall and API policy. Physical attacks test the second deployment decision: what an adversary can observe or modify by touching the device, sensor, memory, firmware, or debug interface. An exposed debug port may permit memory reads, a replacement sensor may supply false inputs, and a writable firmware interface may change execution. Encryption and authentication remain useful when their keys and enforcement mechanisms stay protected; the threat model must identify which physical paths bypass those protections.

The failure mode depends on what the attacker can touch. Replacing a drone’s navigation module, swapping the sensor of a biometric access system, or misaligning a vehicle’s cameras changes system behavior without changing a single model weight. In edge fleets such as the phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet), the coordinator does not control clients’ physical environments. Device ownership does not automatically defeat protected storage or execution, but the coordinator cannot infer the integrity of a client’s data or updates from ownership or enrollment alone.

Internal components create the same risk at a lower layer. A hardware trojan inserted during chip fabrication can remain dormant until a specific input or state triggers it, then leak outputs, corrupt computation, or degrade performance in ways that are difficult to diagnose after deployment. Memory chips and accelerator buses can expose model parameters or training data when an attacker has physical access. Data centers are not exempt. An implant installed by someone with sufficient facility access can monitor administrative credentials or data streams and provide a persistent path into training and inference pipelines.

The defensive implication is that physical-access analysis belongs in the system architecture rather than solely in device packaging. Disabling production debug interfaces closes one access path; signed firmware and secure boot constrain which code can execute. Tamper detection can signal interference, while attestation and supply chain checks provide evidence about measured state and component provenance. These controls address different parts of the trust boundary, so none alone establishes that sensor inputs or runtime computations remain correct after deployment.

13.7.3 Fault injection attacks

A timed voltage glitch or laser pulse on a microcontroller can skip a single assembly jump instruction in a ReLU layer, zeroing out an activation and forcing a safety-critical misclassification without altering a single stored weight (Breier et al. 2018). Fault injection is the active version of the physical-access decision: the attacker does not replace the model artifact but changes the computation while it runs. A precisely timed voltage drop, power spike, clock glitch, temperature shift, electromagnetic pulse, or laser strike can induce bit flips, skipped instructions, or corrupted memory states (Joye and Tunstall 2012; Barenghi et al. 2010; Hutter et al. 2009; Amiel et al. 2006; Skorobogatov 2009; Skorobogatov and Anderson 2003). For ML systems, those faults can force incorrect outputs, bypass security checks, degrade reliability, or expose internal state for later reverse engineering.

Joye, Marc, and Michael Tunstall. 2012. Fault Analysis in Cryptography. Inf. Secur. Cryptography. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-29656-7.
Barenghi, A., G. M. Bertoni, L. Breveglieri, M. Pellicioli, and G. Pelosi. 2010. “Low Voltage Fault Attacks to AES.” 2010 IEEE International Symposium on Hardware-Oriented Security and Trust (HOST), 7–12. https://doi.org/10.1109/hst.2010.5513121.
Hutter, Michael, Jorn-Marc Schmidt, and Thomas Plos. 2009. “Contact-Based Fault Injections and Power Analysis on RFID Tags.” 2009 European Conference on Circuit Theory and Design, 409–12. https://doi.org/10.1109/ecctd.2009.5275012.
Amiel, Frederic, Christophe Clavier, and Michael Tunstall. 2006. “Fault Analysis of DPA-Resistant Algorithms.” In Fault Diagnosis and Tolerance in Cryptography. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/11889700_20.
Skorobogatov, S. 2009. “Local Heating Attacks on Flash Memory Devices.” 2009 IEEE International Workshop on Hardware-Oriented Security and Trust, 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/hst.2009.5225028.
Skorobogatov, S. P., and R. J. Anderson. 2003. “Optical Fault Induction Attacks.” In Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems - CHES 2002. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-36400-5_2.

The ML-specific risk is that a small computation fault can become a semantic failure. An embedded classifier running on a microcontroller may misclassify a safety-important input, while a fault in memory or control logic may expose proprietary weights or architecture details. Unlike ordinary random faults, adversarially timed faults are chosen to land on computations the model or security protocol depends on.

The experiments of Breier et al. (2018) targeted activation-function implementations on a microcontroller with timed laser faults. Figure 16 identifies the vulnerable instruction in the observed ReLU implementation. For a positive accumulator, the copy instructions assign the activation to the output, and the following jmp end normally skips the zeroing block. A laser pulse timed to suppress that jump makes execution fall through into the clear instructions, overwriting the positive output with zero and forcing the neuron inactive. The conditional brge instruction is not the skipped instruction in this example, and the fault changes executed control flow rather than any stored model weight.

Breier, Jakub, Xiaolu Hou, Dirmanto Jap, Lei Ma, Shivam Bhasin, and Yang Liu. 2018. “Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks.” Proceedings of the 2018 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security abs/1806.05859: 2204–6. https://doi.org/10.1145/3243734.3278519.

Fault injection attacks can also be combined with side-channel analysis, where attackers first observe power or timing characteristics to infer model structure or data flow. This reconnaissance helps them time faults against specific layers or operations, such as activation functions or final decision layers. The resulting effect still depends on the implementation, the induced fault, and any checks that detect or contain it.

Embedded and edge ML systems can be vulnerable when exposed hardware combines with resource constraints that limit runtime defenses. Access to system buses, memory, or power supplies can give attackers opportunities to induce faults, even when software access controls remain intact. The relevant protection comes from the device and execution stack: a lightweight model does not itself establish whether memory has error correction, computations have redundant checks, or packaging resists probing.

The defense must combine physical hardening with runtime evidence. Tamper-resistant packaging restricts access, while design obfuscation makes targets harder to locate without itself preventing interference. Error-correcting memory and redundant checks can detect or correct some induced errors; secure firmware constrains code changes but does not prevent a fault during execution. Model-output and sensor-consistency monitors can catch some fault-induced behavior that escapes lower layers; MAVFI demonstrates this pattern for micro-aerial-vehicle workloads with anomaly detection and recovery (Hsiao et al. 2023). These protections are hardest in cost- and power-constrained edge systems, where extra cryptographic hardware or redundancy may be unaffordable, so resilience has to be designed across the electrical, firmware, software, and system layers.

Hsiao, Yu-Shun, Zishen Wan, Tianyu Jia, Radhika Ghosal, Abdulrahman Mahmoud, Arijit Raychowdhury, David Brooks, Gu-Yeon Wei, and Vijay Janapa Reddi. 2023. “MAVFI: An End-to-End Fault Analysis Framework with Anomaly Detection and Recovery for Micro Aerial Vehicles.” 2023 Design, Automation & Test in Europe Conference & Exhibition (DATE), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.23919/date56975.2023.10137246.
Gnad, D. R. E., F. Oboril, and M. B. Tahoori. 2017. “Voltage Drop-Based Fault Attacks on FPGAs Using Valid Bitstreams.” 2017 27th International Conference on Field Programmable Logic and Applications (FPL), 1–7. https://doi.org/10.23919/fpl.2017.8056840.

A data center fleet rarely faces a laser, but it faces the same class of failure in two other forms. Without any attacker, marginal processors corrupt computation silently at fleet scale. With an attacker, shared electrical resources can provide a path for interference. Co-tenants on a shared FPGA have induced timing faults remotely by drawing enough current to drop the supply voltage (Gnad et al. 2017). The check-and-verify defenses of Check-and-Verify Defenses Against Silent Data Corruption can therefore serve security as well as reliability. Their security coverage requires separate evaluation, however, because an attacker may target both the computation and its check rather than induce the independent errors a reliability analysis assumes.

↩︎ Silent data corruption from probabilistic hardware faults at fleet scale is established in The physics of silent corruption.

13.7.4 Side-channel attacks

Even when every network port and debug interface is locked down, variations in power draw, electromagnetic emissions, or cache timing during a forward pass can reveal secret keys, layer topologies, or user inputs (Kocher et al. 1999; Gandolfi et al. 2001). Side-channel attacks test the third deployment decision: whether computation is observable through physical or shared-resource signals when explicit interfaces are sealed. Measuring and analyzing power, electromagnetic, timing, or acoustic signals lets an attacker infer internal state or recover secret data without exploiting any software or network vulnerability.

Kocher, Paul, Joshua Jaffe, and Benjamin Jun. 1999. “Differential Power Analysis.” In Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO’ 99. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48405-1_25.
Gandolfi, Karine, Christophe Mourtel, and Francis Olivier. 2001. “Electromagnetic Analysis: Concrete Results.” In Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems — CHES 2001. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-44709-1_21.

ML accelerators executing inference are exposed to physical leakage as other computing devices are. A matrix multiplication on an edge accelerator can draw current in a pattern correlated with the weight values and input activations being processed. An attacker who can measure that signal may infer properties of the computation, but recovery depends on measurement quality, implementation details, and knowledge or control of inputs. Additional samples help only if the observable signal carries the relevant information. The side-channel surface for a deployed model therefore encompasses both the cryptographic operations protecting its keys and the inference computation itself.

Studies of Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) implementations showed that an implementation can leak information about a key without an attacker breaking the cipher’s mathematical construction. The same distinction between an algorithm and its implementation applies to the ReLU activations, softmax normalizations, and weight-load sequences that constitute a forward pass.

Power analysis of a password check shows the mechanism in its simplest form (Kocher et al. 2011). A device that compares a 5-byte password one byte at a time draws a stable power profile while the bytes match, and figure 17 shows the trace jump at the first wrong byte, where the device halts the comparison.

Kocher, Paul, Joshua Jaffe, Benjamin Jun, and Pankaj Rohatgi. 2011. “Introduction to Differential Power Analysis.” Journal of Cryptographic Engineering 1 (1): 5–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13389-011-0006-y.

The position of the jump reveals how many leading bytes are correct, so repeated guesses collapse a search over all \(256^5\) strings into five searches of 256 values each. ML inference can expose analogous data-dependent behavior when a microcontroller branches on a ReLU input’s sign or hardware skips zero values, producing signals correlated with activation sparsity. Recovering layer topology or parameters from such a signal requires a further inference step supported by the implementation and the available measurements.

The underlying lesson is physical. Computation emits signals, whether as the sound of a cipher machine (Wright and Greengrass 1987) or of a laptop running a cipher (Genkin et al. 2017), the clicks of a keyboard (Asonov and Agrawal 2004), or the current drawn by a processor. For a fleet, the important variant needs no probe at all. On shared hardware, the shared resource itself becomes the measurement instrument. Researchers built a power monitor from logic in their own region of an FPGA shared among users and used it to recover a cryptographic key computed in another user’s region (Zhao and Suh 2018). The sharing that makes multi-tenancy economical turns caches, memory bandwidth, and power delivery into channels between tenants.

Wright, Peter, and Paul Greengrass. 1987. Spycatcher: The Candid Autobiography of a Senior Intelligence Officer. Viking Penguin.
Genkin, Daniel, Adi Shamir, and Eran Tromer. 2017. “Acoustic Cryptanalysis.” Journal of Cryptology 30: 392–443. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-015-9224-2.
Asonov, Dmitri, and Rakesh Agrawal. 2004. “Keyboard Acoustic Emanations.” IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2004. Proceedings. 2004, 3–11. https://doi.org/10.1109/secpri.2004.1301311.
Zhao, M., and G. E. Suh. 2018. “FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks.” 2018 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 229–44. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2018.00049.

Machine learning systems inherit this risk when accelerators or edge devices process sensitive data near an observable signal. A local speech-recognition device may leak timing or power patterns correlated with commands. An accelerator may reveal layer structure, parameter access patterns, or batch shape through timing, power, or electromagnetic traces. Side-channel defense therefore asks which signals are observable in the deployment environment and whether shielding, constant-time execution, noise, monitoring, or physical access controls can reduce the signal enough to preserve the trust boundary.

Learned side-channel analysis

Machine learning also changes the attacker’s side of this analysis. Extracting a key from noisy power traces requires finding signal patterns associated with secret-dependent computations, and a convolutional neural network can learn those patterns from labeled traces, turning part of the analysis into a learned classification task. The attacker still needs suitable measurements and training data, but can reuse the trained model across repeated attempts under compatible conditions. The SCAAML framework (Side-Channel Attacks Assisted with Machine Learning), developed by researchers at Google, is a widely studied and reproducible demonstration of this learned pipeline (Bursztein et al. 2024; Bursztein and Picod 2019).

Bursztein, Elie, Luca Invernizzi, Karel Král, Daniel Moghimi, Jean-Michel Picod, and Marina Zhang. 2024. “Generalized Power Attacks Against Crypto Hardware Using Long-Range Deep Learning.” IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems 2024 (3): 472–99. https://doi.org/10.46586/tches.v2024.i3.472-499.

Power drawn during an AES S-box substitution depends on the data being processed (figure 18). The left panel places a possible leakage interval within a longer trace; the right panel magnifies a schematic difference between processed values. Hamming weight counts the ones in a binary value: 1111 has weight 4, 0101 has weight 2, and 0000 has weight 0. The drawing orders amplitudes by that weight to illustrate a leakage model, not a measured law of CMOS switching. Actual leakage depends on circuit structure, state transitions, noise, and countermeasures. A classifier must learn a reproducible relationship in measured traces before these differences can support key recovery.

Statistical methods use an explicit leakage model. A neural network instead learns features from labeled traces, and its predictions of an intermediate value are combined across traces to score candidate key bytes. This works only if the learned relationship generalizes to traces not used in training.

In a SCAAML guide, Bursztein and Picod (2019) used convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to recover AES keys from power traces collected on an STM32F415 microcontroller running the open-source TinyAES implementation. The models predicted intermediate values of the AES algorithm, such as the output of the S-box9 in the first round, from power traces. The demonstration recovered a full 128-bit key by combining byte-level predictions. Its target was an unprotected implementation, so the number of traces it needed sets no expectation for devices with masking, shuffling, or other countermeasures.

Bursztein, Elie, and Jean-Michel Picod. 2019. “A Hacker Guide to Deep Learning Based Side Channel Attacks.” In DEF CON 27, edited by DEF CON. DEF CON.

9 S-box (substitution box): The nonlinear byte-substitution table in AES. In the first round, its input combines a plaintext byte with a key byte. Predicting its output is a 256-way classification problem; with the corresponding plaintext byte known, the attacker can map predictions back to candidate key bytes and combine evidence across traces.

Learned side-channel models can reduce the analysis effort or trace count of an attack when suitable training data and measurable leakage are available. In a fleet built from a few part numbers, reusable attack models create correlated risk. Transfer still requires evaluation across devices, firmware, measurement conditions, and countermeasures; matching part numbers alone do not guarantee it. The defensive response must therefore address both the attacker’s access to measurements and the leakage of the computation itself.

13.7.5 Leaky interfaces

Whereas side-channel attacks leak through unintended physical signals, leaky interfaces expose information or accept unverified inputs through diagnostic, update, and communication channels the system already provides. An exposed baseboard management controller in a data center rack or an active JTAG port on a field camera allows an attacker to read memory or rewrite firmware while bypassing every OS and model-layer defense, placing leaky interfaces directly between physical access and lifecycle trust.

A leaky interface is any access point that reveals more information than intended or accepts commands from the wrong actor. The common causes are weak authentication, missing encryption, inadequate isolation, and development interfaces left exposed in production. Consumer, medical, and industrial systems have repeatedly shown the pattern: Wi-Fi-enabled baby monitors have exposed unsecured remote access ports,10 and pacemaker vulnerabilities11 have shown how wireless interfaces can become safety-critical control channels. Debug ports12 left enabled on production devices are the canonical hardware case: a consumer smart lightbulb, for example, exposed unencrypted Wi-Fi credentials through such a port, giving attackers a path into the home network without defeating any network defense.

10 IoT device vulnerabilities: Default credentials, unencrypted communications, and outdated firmware create access paths into connected devices. A compromised smart camera can supply manipulated inputs or participate in distributed attacks; if it also contributes training data or federated updates, that path can carry poisoning attempts. The consequences depend on the device’s role and permissions.

11 Medical device security: Connected medical devices require secure maintenance over long operating lifetimes. In a device that uses ML, compromised inputs, weights, or preprocessing can alter clinical behavior without stopping the device. Traditional device software can also fail silently, so the additional ML requirement is to evaluate learned behavior alongside firmware integrity and physical safety controls.

12 Debug port vulnerabilities: JTAG and Serial Wire Debug can expose memory and execution control when debug access remains enabled and authorized checks are absent or bypassed. An attacker may then recover weights accessible in plaintext, but an exposed connector alone does not defeat correctly enforced debug locks or encryption whose keys remain unavailable.

The data center has its own privileged maintenance interfaces. A server’s baseboard management controller commonly supports power control, console access, and firmware management over an out-of-band network, independently of the host operating system. Compromising its credentials or firmware can therefore expose control paths that host access policies do not govern. The resulting reach depends on network segmentation, controller privileges, and firmware-update protections. The attestation checks of section 13.6.4 help only when trusted measurements cover the affected components and the attacker cannot forge the evidence or alter the verifier’s approved state. The same reasoning applies at the edge, where a maintenance interface that lacks authentication can expose user data, alter model weights, or disable security features.

Securing interfaces is therefore inventory work as much as cryptography. Strong authentication, encrypted communication, anomaly detection, access-control policy, periodic audit, and zero-trust defaults all serve the same principle: every interface must justify what it exposes and who can use it.

13.7.6 Supply chain risks

Supply chain risks extend the provenance decision from exposed maintenance interfaces to every hardware and software component across every stage of its life. A counterfeit memory module, modified network interface card (NIC) firmware, or compromised open-source dependency replicated across 128 cluster nodes introduces a backdoor before the first training job even starts. The smallest unit of this risk is the counterfeit part. A counterfeit processor, memory module, sensor, or network device may look and function like a genuine one while degrading faster, failing under load, or containing hidden circuitry, so procurement becomes part of the security boundary. Organizations that unknowingly deploy such parts may also violate safety, privacy, or cybersecurity obligations, which makes component provenance evidence that the deployed system matches the certified one.

A component’s life runs through design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, and deployment (figure 19), and each stage presents opportunities for tampering or substitution. Recycled electronic waste can be relabeled as new, distributors can mix cloned parts into legitimate shipments, and insiders at manufacturing facilities can embed hardware trojans that routine functional tests may miss. Micrography, X-ray screening, and functional testing provide different evidence, with coverage and cost determined by the suspected modification. Procurement therefore needs risk-based provenance controls as well as inspection; passing a functional test does not establish a component’s origin or exclude dormant malicious behavior.

Fleet procurement changes the shape of this risk. A training cluster is bought in bulk from a small number of part numbers, so each of the 128 nodes of the reference cluster carries the same accelerators, network adapters, management controller, and firmware images as every other. A compromised shared design, firmware release, or production batch can therefore affect many nodes at once. Replication does not remove a vulnerability shared by the replicas, although one compromised unit is evidence about its part number, not proof that every unit carrying it is affected. The provenance bound on trust (principle 22) applies to silicon and firmware as much as to data. Supplier, batch, and firmware records help identify the affected population; supplier concentration increases common dependencies even when those records are complete.

Hardware compromise also changes the economics of response. Software vulnerabilities can often be patched remotely, but a hardware compromise that slips past every check to deployment (figure 19) may require physical replacement. That possibility adds replacement cost, service interruption, and revalidation to the expected loss and strengthens the case for preventive checks before deployment.

A disputed 2018 report of surveillance chips implanted on server motherboards, which the named companies publicly denied (Robertson and Riley 2018), shows why allegations must be separated from verified compromise. A claim about deployed components needs evidence from the relevant fabrication, assembly, distribution, and integration stages, and component validation, runtime monitoring, attestation, and hardware roots of trust each supply part of that evidence.

Robertson, J., and M. Riley. 2018. The Big Hack: How China Used a Tiny Chip to Infiltrate U.S. Companies - Bloomberg.

The engineering takeaway is that hardware trust must be evidenced continuously across design, fabrication, procurement, deployment, and retirement. A trusted execution environment (TEE) isolates selected code and data from parts of the surrounding host. Attestation supplies cryptographic evidence about that protected environment before another component entrusts it with secrets. Neither mechanism establishes that a model is behaviorally correct, and both depend on an explicit set of trusted hardware and software components.

Checkpoint 13.3: Knowledge check: Hardware security

Before moving from hardware threats to the defenses anchored in hardware, check that each vulnerability family is attached to the deployment decision it tests.

These hardware threats endanger the model, its data, and the execution environment that protects them. They also set the limit of every software control examined so far, because each of those controls assumes that some layer beneath it remains trustworthy. A defense architecture must therefore state which components it trusts and what each layer adds when another fails.

Self-Check: Question

  1. Vulnerabilities like Meltdown and Spectre exploit transient execution in modern processors. What microarchitectural mechanism can let an attacker infer protected data across an intended isolation boundary?

    1. Transient instructions can encode protected data in cache state that remains measurable after the processor discards their architectural effects.
    2. Speculative execution permanently overwrites physical DRAM cells with ciphertext keys without notifying the OS kernel.
    3. The CPU floating-point unit truncates FP32 tensor activations to INT8 during branch prediction.
    4. Speculative branch predictors disable hardware-level AES encryption engines on PCIe accelerator interconnects.

  2. In laser fault injection experiments on embedded neural network microcontrollers (e.g., Breier et al., 2018), researchers targeted the assembly instructions implementing the ReLU activation function. Explain the assembly-level mechanism of this attack and its effect on the model’s output.

  3. An attacker places an oscilloscope probe near the power rail of an edge ML microcontroller running a proprietary convolutional network. How can the attacker infer model architecture or recover layer weights without accessing the device’s firmware or API?

    1. By sending malformed TCP packets that trigger core dumps over the microcontroller’s UART interface.
    2. By measuring instruction-dependent power consumption waveforms where current draw varies with weight values, multiplication operand hamming weights, and ReLU pre-activation signs.
    3. By overwriting the microcontroller’s secure boot ROM keys using over-the-air firmware updates.
    4. By inducing thermal shutdown to force the microcontroller to reboot into an unauthenticated recovery bootloader.

  4. True or False: A production edge device exposes an unauthenticated JTAG/SWD interface that permits reads of plaintext model weights in flash. Physical access to that interface can bypass host software permissions for those reads.

  5. Place the five stages of the hardware supply chain in sequential order from initial creation to operational deployment:

  1. Fabrication: Silicon wafer processing and packaging where hardware trojans can be inserted into ASIC masks
  2. Distribution: Shipping, warehousing, and logistics where physical tampering or component substitution can occur
  3. Design: Architecture specification and RTL creation where design flaws or backdoors can be introduced
  4. Deployment: Integration into production servers and edge fleets where counterfeit parts manifest operational failures
  5. Assembly: PCB assembly and soldering where inferior or cloned components can be substituted

  1. Traditional side-channel cryptanalysis required expert analysts to manually filter noise, align oscilloscope waveforms, and apply statistical correlation power analysis. What key capability do convolutional neural networks provide when applied to side-channel trace analysis?

    1. They mathematically break 256-bit AES encryption keys in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time without requiring physical measurement traces.
    2. They replace hardware security modules with software-only virtual enclaves that simulate quantum annealing.
    3. They learn leakage features from labeled traces and predict secret-dependent intermediate values, which an attacker combines with known inputs to score candidate keys.
    4. They prevent the physical device from consuming electrical power during sensitive cryptographic operations.

See Answers →

13.8 Comprehensive Defense Architectures

An adversary who bypasses an API rate limit may still face authorization checks, restricted outputs, or an isolated execution environment. These controls protect different assets and constrain different actions. Secure ML systems use defense in depth to limit what follows from a failed mechanism. The benefit depends on whether the remaining controls retain their enforcement power; several checks that share the same compromised credential or runtime do not provide independent barriers.

Countermeasures fall into four architectural tiers (figure 20). Hardware mechanisms include trusted execution environments, secure boot, HSM key custody, and physical unclonable function (PUF) device identities. Platform controls include container isolation, network segmentation, access control, and runtime telemetry. The model layer includes adversarial training, input validation, output monitoring, and rate limiting, while data-layer controls include differential privacy, encryption at rest, provenance tracking, and secure aggregation. These tiers partition defenses by the layer they protect, which differs from the data, model, interface, and infrastructure layers of section 13.4.1.1 that partition where an adversary enters. The two maps line up except at the interface. Interface controls such as rate limiting, input validation, and output monitoring guard the model’s query boundary, so the stack files them with the model tier. The serving platform beneath enforces them, which is why the runtime-monitoring discussion below treats them as platform mechanisms. Infrastructure threats fall to the hardware and platform tiers. The dependency arrow highlights the runtime support that many controls require. A compromised host can expose raw records or alter a privacy mechanism before release, but it does not retroactively invalidate the differential privacy guarantee of an artifact already produced by a correctly implemented mechanism. The dependency analysis must identify the protected asset and release, not assume that every control fails together.

Layered defense (also known as defense in depth) makes these dependencies explicit. Differential privacy bounds what a specified release reveals about an individual’s contribution; it does not protect a separate copy of raw training records from theft. Federated learning changes where training data reside but does not, by itself, bound what updates reveal. Hardware isolation can protect execution within its threat model without establishing that an application follows the intended data policy. Combining these mechanisms requires stating each guarantee and checking which assumptions the other layers preserve.

The stack also orders the dependencies. A rate limit enforced by the serving platform is only as reliable as that platform, and the platform is only as reliable as the firmware and processor it runs on. Trust therefore builds from the bottom tier upward. Silicon anchors it, platform controls govern how a model is deployed and monitored, model-tier choices shape the learned function itself, and the data layer determines what a correctly computed release reveals.

13.8.1 Hardware security foundations

Anchoring the bottom tier of that stack in silicon matters because software-only access controls and encrypted disks cannot protect plaintext model weights or keys in RAM once an attacker gains root access on a host OS or cloud hypervisor. Software checks enforced solely by a compromised operating system can be disabled or falsified, and an unlocked debug interface can similarly expose execution state that software policy was intended to protect. Controls enforced in a separate hardware trust domain remain effective even when the operating system, runtime, or application code is compromised, which motivates identifying exactly where each security decision is made and who can alter it.

Hardware-based security creates a root of trust anchored in silicon, giving higher-layer defenses a foundation that host software cannot rewrite. Machine learning systems deployed in edge devices, embedded systems, and untrusted cloud infrastructure often depend on that anchor because the attacker may have physical access, co-tenant access, or administrative access to parts of the stack.

The trust boundary becomes especially important when systems must satisfy regulatory requirements. Healthcare ML systems handling protected health information under HIPAA must implement technical safeguards such as access control, audit controls, integrity protection, and transmission security. Systems processing personal data within GDPR’s territorial and material scope must also demonstrate appropriate technical and organizational measures, including data-protection-by-design principles. Hardware security does not satisfy these requirements alone, but it provides the boot, runtime, key-management, and device-identity guarantees that software controls often assume.

Four hardware security mechanisms divide that foundation by separating startup integrity, runtime isolation, key custody, and device identity. Secure boot verifies whether the system started from authentic code, whereas trusted execution environments (TEEs) isolate sensitive computation while it runs on an untrusted host. Because both mechanisms rely on cryptographic keys and device identity, hardware security modules (HSMs) generate and use keys without exposing them to ordinary memory, and physical unclonable functions (PUFs) derive a hardware-bound identity that is harder to copy than a software credential. Table 7 compares the four primitives after each has been examined; they work best when composed across hardware, firmware, and software boundaries rather than selected as standalone products.

Trusted execution environments

A TEE is first a trust-boundary decision: which parts of the model, key material, input data, or attestation path must remain protected even if the surrounding host is compromised. A trusted execution environment (TEE) is the hardware-isolated processor region that implements that boundary. TEEs enforce confidentiality, integrity, and runtime isolation within a stated threat model. Their guarantee depends on the trusted hardware, firmware, and code inside the protected boundary; isolating a vulnerable application does not make that application correct.

For machine learning, a TEE can keep model parameters and sensitive inputs confidential during inference and protect execution from host-level tampering. It can, for example, prevent malicious software on the same device from extracting model parameters, or keep computations on facial or fingerprint data inside the protected boundary. Correct execution of an approved model says nothing about whether its predictions are accurate or safe.

Isolation of this kind appears at two scales. On consumer devices, a dedicated security coprocessor such as Apple’s Secure Enclave keeps credentials and biometric features protected even if the application processor kernel is compromised (Apple 2024b). In the data center, the relevant form is the confidential virtual machine, which protects an entire guest, including its model weights and user inputs, from the hypervisor and host operators, and which the fleet admits into a job only after remote attestation (section 13.6.4).

Remote attestation supports the distributed trust decision: before components exchange sensitive data or model updates, a verifier checks fresh evidence about measured code and its hardware-protected boundary against an admission policy. Binding a communication key to that evidence connects the accepted identity to the ensuing channel. Attestation alone does not establish the correctness of every runtime operation. For ML, protection follows the computation: inputs, weights, and activations remain covered only while their processing and storage stay within the chosen boundary.

TEE implementations combine execution isolation, protected memory, integrity mechanisms, and protected key storage in different ways. The isolation boundary may surround an application region, a secure processor mode, or an entire virtual machine. Access controls restrict which principals can read protected state, while memory encryption and authentication can extend protection beyond the processor boundary where the architecture supports them. Persistent storage needs its own protection when data leave protected memory. Within the execution boundary, computation uses plaintext directly. The deployment analysis must therefore trace where plaintext exists, which components can access it, and which integrity and freshness checks the platform actually supplies.

Platforms differ mainly in the size of the protected boundary. ARM TrustZone13 splits a mobile or embedded processor into secure and normal worlds. Intel SGX isolates individual enclaves inside an application’s address space on servers. Confidential virtual machines such as those built on AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX move the boundary out to a whole guest operating system, which lets unmodified ML serving stacks run inside it at the cost of a larger trusted code base.

13 ARM TrustZone: Introduced in 2004, TrustZone partitions an ARM processor into secure and normal “worlds” with hardware-enforced isolation. Its presence on a device does not by itself protect an ML deployment: the model, keys, and data path must actually be placed inside the secure world, which depends on whether the device vendor exposes secure-world applications beyond key storage.

Apple. 2024a. Facial Matching Security. Apple Platform Security.

Apple’s system-on-chip (SoC) Secure Enclave shows these boundaries in silicon (figure 21). Its dedicated processor, true random number generator (TRNG), public key accelerator (PKA), and cryptographic engines operate separately from the application processor, which communicates through a mailbox interface. A memory protection engine encrypts and authenticates the enclave’s external memory, while protected key paths support storage encryption (Apple 2024b). On consumer devices, Apple’s Face ID applies this architecture by binding its biometric templates and comparison logic to the Secure Enclave rather than treating them as ordinary application data (Apple 2024a). This example demonstrates isolation of designated security operations and state; it does not imply that arbitrary application model weights or activations reside inside the Secure Enclave, because their protection depends on the execution and data paths the platform supports.

Trusted execution environments carry costs in every C³ dimension. Protected memory, memory encryption, and transitions between trusted and untrusted modes can add compute and latency, and battery-powered devices also pay in energy for secure memory accesses and cryptographic work. Development cost rises because code inside the boundary must follow isolation, attestation, and update protocols, and some deployments must also pass formal certification such as Common Criteria. Distributed training and federated inference add coordination work when their admission policy requires attestation and protected key exchange. A central verifier can perform admission checks; direct mutual attestation between every pair is not inherently required. TEEs therefore fit deployments whose threat model, whether adversarial users, cloud co-tenants, or malicious insiders, justifies that investment.

Protected-memory and overhead budgets

Hardware security features are budgeted like any other resource. Each primitive spends time at its boundary crossings and capacity in its protected memory, and both costs must be sized before a design commits to a primitive. Hardware security overhead must be measured for the chosen implementation. A secure-world transition has a cost per transition, not automatically a cost per inference: the result depends on how often the inference path crosses the boundary and what data it copies. Encryption, cache effects, and paging add separate costs. Energy overhead requires power and elapsed-time measurements; it cannot be inferred from a transition-latency figure alone.

Memory is the second budget. The protected working set competes for platform-specific memory capacity. Some implementations support protected paging beyond resident capacity, so overflow can impose substantial movement costs rather than an absolute model-size limit. Compression or partitioning changes those costs and may also change which values remain protected.

Security features scale differently than computational resources. Protected memory capacity, not host memory, sets how much of a model can remain resident inside a TEE without paging. On an older Intel SGX configuration with a 128 MB enclave page cache (the protected resident memory), ResNet-50’s FP32 weights alone would fill about 76.2 percent of it. A ResNet-18 model is about 46.8 MB with FP32 weights or 11.7 MB with INT8 weights, while ResNet-50 is about 102.2 MB with FP32 weights or 25.6 MB with INT8 weights before activations and runtime buffers. The fleet’s reference model sits far beyond that scale. The FP16 weights of the Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) model occupy as many bytes as the 350 GB gradient it reduces each step, orders of magnitude more than an enclave page cache. Fleet-scale confidential computing therefore draws its boundary around a whole confidential virtual machine, an entire guest protected from the host, rather than an application enclave.

FP32 ResNet-50 weights alone nearly fill an older enclave page cache.

Different threat models and protection levels require quantitative trade-off analysis. Encryption and authentication are distinct operations, and AES encryption alone does not verify integrity. An authenticated mode or a separate authentication mechanism is needed when tampering is in scope, and the latency must be measured for the actual data volume and hardware.

TEE assurance depends on its protected initialization and attestation path, not merely on when the host boots. Some enclave designs explicitly tolerate an untrusted host operating system, while other trusted environments depend on a verified platform startup chain. Secure boot complements these boundaries by authenticating the components included in that chain; the threat model must identify which firmware and initialization code remain trusted.

Secure boot

Secure boot is a mechanism that ensures a device only boots software components that are cryptographically verified under the platform’s configured trust policy. At startup, each stage of the boot process, comprising the bootloader, kernel, and base operating system, is checked against a known-good digital signature. If any signature fails verification, the boot sequence is halted, blocking components that fail authentication. The chain rests on a trusted initial stage; signed but vulnerable software remains a risk.

A compromised boot process, particularly on embedded or edge hardware, can load malicious software before the ML runtime begins, enabling attackers to intercept model weights, tamper with training data, or reroute inference results. Such breaches can lead to incorrect or manipulated predictions, unauthorized data access, or device repurposing for botnets or crypto-mining.

For machine learning systems, secure boot authenticates the components included in its verification chain. Model artifacts receive this protection only when a verified loader checks their signatures or a signed manifest before loading them; boot verification alone does not authenticate weights read later from storage. Secure update flows must extend the same verification policy to replacement firmware, runtimes, and model artifacts.

Secure boot frequently operates in tandem with hardware-based TEEs to establish an unbroken chain of trust prior to code execution. The chain is a stepped verification handshake that pairs each trusted execution stage with an explicit cryptographic authentication gate (Regenscheid 2018), as figure 22 traces. Execution proceeds from an immutable boot root through a verified bootloader and operating system, halting and rejecting the component if any signature check fails. For machine learning pipelines, Stage 3 extends this chain beyond conventional system software: the verified OS or loader authenticates the model manifest and artifact digest before launching the authorized ML workload. The terminal stage emphasizes that while boot-time authentication blocks unauthorized or tampered binaries, dynamic runtime controls remain necessary to guard against post-boot attacks and data-dependent exploits.

Regenscheid, Andrew. 2018. Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines. NIST SP 800-193. National Institute of Standards; Technology. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-193.

Startup trust is what makes the runtime isolation described earlier meaningful, and it must survive updates. Apple’s signed boot chain verifies the Secure Enclave firmware before any biometric data is processed and installs only software versions Apple is still signing, so a secure initial boot keeps its assumptions only through a controlled update path (Apple 2021a, 2024b, 2021b).

Apple. 2021a. Boot Process for iPad and iPhone Devices. Apple Platform Security.
Apple. 2024b. The Secure Enclave. Apple Platform Security.
Apple. 2021b. Secure Software Updates. Apple Platform Security.

Secure boot also creates key-management and lifecycle obligations. Enterprises must protect signing keys, distribute trusted verification material, and support revocation or recovery when an authorized key is compromised. The affected trust chain depends on that key’s authority and the platform’s recovery design. Verification adds startup work, and every component covered by the policy must remain authenticated through updates, whether by an individual signature or a digest bound into an authenticated manifest. The deployment must identify which components the chain actually covers.

At fleet scale, device identity and evidence of startup state support distinct admission decisions. The Device Identifier Composition Engine (Trusted Computing Group 2018) combines a device secret with software measurements to derive identities tied to the measured state. IEEE 802.1AR (IEEE 802.1 Working Group 2018) defines cryptographically bound device identities and their provisioning; a device identity alone does not establish which software is running. Fleet attestation (section 13.6.4) connects authenticated identity with acceptable state evidence before a node receives keys or joins a job.

Trusted Computing Group. 2018. Hardware Requirements for a Device Identifier Composition Engine. Family 2.0, Level 00, Revision 78. Trusted Computing Group.
IEEE 802.1 Working Group. 2018. IEEE Standard for Local and Metropolitan Area Networks—Secure Device Identity. IEEE Std 802.1AR-2018.

Secure boot, when extended through the model loader and complemented by controlled updates, can establish that the configured authority approved the loaded components. Correct model behavior and freedom from vulnerabilities in the authenticated software remain separate claims. Runtime isolation and monitoring address different parts of that assurance argument.

Hardware security modules

While TEEs and secure boot provide runtime isolation and integrity verification, hardware security modules (HSMs) specialize in the cryptographic operations that underpin these protections. An HSM is a tamper-resistant physical device designed to perform cryptographic operations and securely manage digital keys. HSMs are standard in finance, defense, and cloud infrastructure; in an ML pipeline they protect the keys on which model integrity and data confidentiality depend.

HSMs provide an isolated, hardened environment for performing sensitive operations such as key generation, digital signing, encryption, and decryption. Unlike general-purpose processors, they are engineered to withstand physical tampering and side-channel attacks, and they typically include protected storage, cryptographic accelerators, and internal audit logging. HSMs may be implemented as standalone appliances, plug-in modules, or integrated chips embedded within broader systems.

In machine learning systems, HSMs can protect signing keys and the keys used to wrap data-encryption keys. The distinction matters because a root key may remain inside the HSM while a workload uses a released data key inside its authorized execution boundary. Two distributed workflows illustrate this role. An HSM can protect the certificate authority’s signing key used to certify enrolled devices; each device then proves possession of its own private key. Secure aggregation does not inherently require an HSM, and an authenticated but compromised client can still submit poisoned gradients. An HSM can also wrap a model-decryption key for a TEE’s attestation-bound public key after the verifier accepts the evidence. Keeping weights out of plaintext host memory then depends on the TEE’s key handling, loader, and execution path, not on the wrapping operation alone.

HSMs also play a role in maintaining the integrity of machine learning models. In many production pipelines, models must be signed before deployment to ensure that only verified versions are accepted into runtime environments. The signing keys used to authenticate models can be stored and managed within the HSM, providing cryptographic assurance that the deployed artifact is authentic and untampered. Similarly, secure firmware updates and configuration changes, regardless of whether they pertain to models, hyperparameters, or supporting infrastructure, can be validated using signatures produced by the HSM.

In addition to protecting inference workloads, HSMs can be used to secure model training. During training, data may originate from distributed and potentially untrusted sources. HSM-backed protocols can help ensure that training pipelines perform encryption, integrity checks, and access control enforcement securely and in compliance with organizational or legal requirements. In regulated industries such as healthcare and finance, such protections are often necessary to satisfy required safeguards. For instance, the HIPAA Security Rule requires technical safeguards such as access control, audit controls, integrity protections, and transmission security, while treating encryption and some integrity controls as addressable implementation specifications. GDPR lists pseudonymization and encryption as examples of appropriate technical and organizational measures where they fit the risk.

HSM deployment introduces a capacity and integration budget. Signing throughput, key-unwrapping latency, and network access to a remote HSM must be measured for the operations actually used, because the HSM sits on the signing and key-release path and its throughput, not the accelerator’s, bounds how fast keys reach the fleet. The protected key boundary can also require changes to application interfaces and fleet provisioning. Certification and procurement requirements, including applicable cryptographic-module standards, constrain which devices and configurations can be used.

HSMs combine key custody with protected cryptographic operations. Resource-constrained embedded systems may need a smaller mechanism for a narrower task: deriving a device-specific secret without storing a persistent copy of that secret. Physical unclonable functions use a chip’s physical properties for this purpose. They can support key derivation and identity, but do not replace the HSM’s full cryptographic processing and policy-enforcement role.

Physical unclonable functions

PUFs14 provide a hardware-intrinsic mechanism for cryptographic key generation and device authentication by exploiting physical randomness in semiconductor fabrication (Gassend et al. 2002). Unlike traditional keys stored in memory, a PUF generates secret values based on microscopic variations in a chip’s physical properties, which are inherent to manufacturing processes and difficult to clone or predict, even by the manufacturer. Because of variation such as doping concentration and line edge roughness, chips fabricated from the same design masks differ measurably in timing or voltage behavior, and a PUF circuit amplifies those differences into a device-dependent response to each input challenge. An attacker may still predict responses from a vulnerable design without physically cloning the chip.

14 PUF (physical unclonable function): Manufacturing variation can support device-specific key derivation without storing a persistent copy of the key. Separate device keys limit the reach of a storage-key compromise, but they do not prevent extraction of plaintext model weights during execution or attacks that predict a vulnerable PUF’s responses.

Gassend, Blaise, Dwaine Clarke, Marten van Dijk, and Srinivas Devadas. 2002. “Silicon Physical Random Functions.” Proceedings of the 9th ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, 148–60. https://doi.org/10.1145/586110.586132.

This challenge-response mechanism allows PUFs to serve several cryptographic purposes. They can be used to derive device-specific keys that never need to be stored externally, reducing the attack surface for key exfiltration. The same mechanism also supports secure authentication and attestation, where devices must prove their identity to trusted servers or hardware gateways. These properties make PUFs a natural fit for machine learning systems deployed in embedded and distributed environments.

For ML fleets, a PUF can reduce the need to inject and persistently store a unique secret in each device. The phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) and the cameras and drones of edge deployments still need enrollment: the verifier must associate a device with trusted authentication evidence and manage its admission and revocation. A PUF-derived key can encrypt the on-device model at rest, so copying the stored file does not yield the device-bound key that decrypts it. Authentication can use enrolled challenge-response information or a credential backed by a derived key, depending on the design. Both protections have limits. Plaintext weights extracted during execution expose the shared model regardless of how the storage key was generated, and successful authentication establishes which device is speaking, not that its runtime software is uncompromised.

Four PUF architectures draw on different physical sources of variation (Gao et al. 2020), as the panels of figure 23 show. In each, two devices of the same design answer challenge \(\PufChallenge\) with different responses (\(\PufResponse_1 \ne \PufResponse_2\)), whether the response is an optical speckle pattern, an arbiter’s response bit \(\PufResponseBit\) set by racing signal paths, or the startup state of an SRAM cell. These responses are not perfectly repeatable under every operating condition, which motivates the error correction and calibration discussed next.

Gao, Y., S. F. Al-Sarawi, and D. Abbott. 2020. “Physical Unclonable Functions.” Nature Electronics 3 (2): 81–91. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41928-020-0372-5.

PUFs also present engineering challenges. Their responses drift with temperature, voltage, and aging, so production designs add error correction or helper data and calibrate devices during fabrication, at some cost in layout area and test time. Managing large sets of challenge-response pairs raises questions of storage, consistency, and revocation, and the statistical structure of some PUF designs makes their responses predictable to machine learning-based modeling attacks if enough pairs are observed. Within those limits, PUFs reduce the key-management burden for large device fleets and supply a hardware-bound identity that complements secure boot, TEEs, and HSMs.

Mechanisms comparison

Trusted execution environments, secure boot, hardware security modules, and physical unclonable functions address distinct layers of the platform rather than substituting for one another. The design choice is which primitive owns which trust boundary, and table 7 sets the four side by side by function, use in ML, and trade-offs.

Together, these hardware primitives support a defense-in-depth strategy for securing ML systems in adversarial environments. Their integration needs an explicit assurance argument: which components remain trusted, which evidence supports that trust, and which attacks fall outside the protection. Safety-sensitive devices and distributed learning systems need this argument as much as they need the mechanisms themselves.

Hardware primitives supply evidence and enforcement for selected platform properties. Deployment controls use those capabilities to decide which model artifacts may load and which callers may use them. The transition from platform assurance to application policy is therefore a composition problem: the loader and serving endpoint must enforce the intended permissions within the protected boundary.

13.8.2 Secure model deployment

Training a robust model inside a locked cluster accomplishes nothing if the exported artifact is packaged as an untrusted pickle file, stored unencrypted, or served behind an API key with no per-principal quota. A trusted platform establishes where a model runs; deployment controls decide who can load it, who can call it, and whether its behavior survives contact with users, operators, and attackers. As models move into edge devices, public APIs, and multi-tenant platforms, serialization, packaging, and endpoint access policies determine whether the integrity, confidentiality, and availability established during training survive inference.

Because section 13.5.1.4 already quantified the API-boundary query quotas, output perturbation, and pricing regimes that counter model extraction, deployment-stage controls here focus on artifact custody, cryptographic packaging, and endpoint authentication infrastructure, while the design-stage controls of section 13.8.4 shape the model’s behavior and ownership evidence. Deployment controls also have to survive ordinary optimization work such as quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation, where performance improvements must not compromise artifact integrity, ownership evidence, or access-control boundaries.

Once training is complete, the model must be securely packaged for deployment. Authenticated encryption protects stored artifacts when its keys remain inside the intended trust boundary; a signed manifest authenticates the expected artifact digest before loading. Obfuscation may raise reverse-engineering effort but does not provide the confidentiality contract of encryption. Runtime key custody and the loader’s verification policy determine whether packaging protection survives execution.

Deployment environments must enforce access policies at inference endpoints. OAuth supplies delegated authorization; mutual TLS authenticates certificate-bearing peers; API keys identify credentials that the service maps to permissions and quotas. Role-based access control (RBAC) can restrict those permissions by operational role. These mechanisms support the query controls in section 13.5.1.4, but a credential is not proof of a unique human or organization. An attacker who can obtain many accounts can still distribute queries across identities, so account issuance, cumulative budgets, and abuse detection remain part of the boundary.

An API key demonstrates possession of a credential and allows the backend to enforce its associated policies. Keeping keys out of source code reduces accidental exposure in version control, but environment variables alone do not prevent leaks through logs, process inspection, or a compromised runtime. Secret retrieval, scoped permissions, rotation, and redacted logging must be designed together. Model verification against an authenticated manifest, input limits, rate controls, and security-event logging complement credential management, while runtime monitoring (section 13.8.3) extends these protections into active operation.

13.8.3 Runtime system monitoring

A model binary that passed cryptographic signature verification at boot can still receive adversarial prompts, drift into unsafe generations, or have its weights modified in memory during operation. Secure deployment controls who can load the model and call the endpoint, while runtime monitoring checks whether the live system is still behaving like the approved system across cloud services, edge devices, and embedded hardware.

Runtime monitoring must decide whether an input should reach the model, whether the output is behaving normally, and whether the serving system is still the one originally deployed. The corresponding mechanisms are input validation, output monitoring, and system integrity checks.

Input validation

Input validation checks incoming data before it reaches a machine learning model. Format and range checks enforce explicit input contracts, while statistical and semantic checks estimate whether an input fits expected conditions. These checks can reject malformed inputs that disrupt preprocessing or inference and some adversarial inputs crafted to trigger incorrect predictions. Passing validation establishes only that the implemented checks accepted the input, not that the model will handle it correctly.

Small, carefully chosen changes to input data can cause models to make high-confidence but incorrect predictions (Goodfellow et al. 2015). Such inputs may satisfy ordinary type and range checks. Input validation therefore complements model robustness evaluation; it cannot replace testing how the learned function behaves on valid but adversarial inputs.

Goodfellow, I. J., J. Shlens, and C. Szegedy. 2015. “Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Validation techniques range from low-level checks of size, type, and value range to semantic filters, such as a face detector on an uploaded image or a speech activity detector on a voice clip. These checks reject inputs that violate the declared contract, but an adversarial input that satisfies the contract still reaches the model, and a semantic filter’s own error rates belong in the validation assessment.

In generative systems, input validation can include prompt filtering against an application’s content policy. A medical education application, for example, might reject requests to generate fabricated treatment claims.
